Built to protect the Google Ads ecosystem and now used by multiple teams across Google, the platform organizes anti-abuse intelligence into a single, interconnected view.

title: How Vodafone is using the Data Engineering Agent to improve their data pipelines
raw_text: For large organizations, building and maintaining data pipelines is one of the most complex tasks that data engineering teams are tasked with. In BigQuery environments, the Data Engineering Agent can help, leveraging Gemini to to automate these workflows. In this blog post, Vodafone Czech Republic describes how it has used the Data Engineering Agent to modernize and optimize BigQuery stored procedures, transforming them into modern data pipelines and reducing pipeline execution times by half. - Pedro Esteves, Google Cloud The Data Engineering Agent makes it easy to build and maintain modern data pipelines. The agent is available in BigQuery pipelines and Dataform . At Vodafone, we used the agent directly in Dataform to build Dataform pipelines. As shown in the example below, the Data Engineering Agent takes natural language instructions together with any code provided in the instruction file to build the Dataform pipeline. How Vodafone currently executes its pipelines Vodafone Czech Republic uses many BigQuery stored procedures to transform data for business purposes. These stored procedures are a legacy of a previous on-premises data warehouse migration to BigQuery. Many of them contain 2,000 or 3,000 lines of code and run sequentially. Compared to a modular Dataform approach created by the Data Engineering Agent, there are several known disadvantages of maintaining legacy, multi-thousand-line stored procedures, as described in the table below. Feature Legacy stored procedures (Monolith) Modular approach (Dataform) Code structure Single file, 1000s of lines, complex logic mixed. Small, modular .sqlx files Logic reuse Copy/Paste code blocks (prone to drift). functions and ref() for strict logic reuse Testing Manual, ad-hoc, rarely done Automated testing (Unique, Not Null, Referential Integrity) built-in Documentation Comments in code (usually outdated) Auto-generated documentation with lineage graph Execution Manual scheduling; hard-coded dependency management Automatic execution based on lineage (DAG) How the Data Engineering Agent improved our data pipelines To solve the problems of running and maintaining legacy stored procedures, we used the Data Engineering Agent to migrate some of the stored procedures into Dataform pipelines. Parallelization of code The Data Engineering Agent was able to parallelize the code into independent steps which are then run in parallel to improve readability and performance. See the example below: Caching intermediate results The Data Engineering Agent can understand dependencies between the tables and cache certain intermediate tables using BigQuery materialized views . This means that tables that are used in downstream processes can be cached, speeding up code execution and reducing cost. Facilitating orchestration of the pipeline Having a modular pipeline allows us to facilitate end-to-end orchestration and pipeline dependencies to meet our SLAs. Before using Dataform, we had to manually control pipeline execution by creating metadata tables with several checkpoints and logs. Dependencies between stored procedures jobs were also maintained manually in a spreadsheet. By executing the pipeline in Dataform, all the dependencies and execution logs are handled by Dataform. Ability to run sections of the pipeline Because the code is now split into several steps, it’s possible to execute only a subset of the actions in Dataform rather than running the entire stored procedure. This can help with debugging and gives us the flexibility to only run the relevant sections of the code. Lessons learned There’s a trade-off between parallelization and caching. When we prompted the Data Engineering Agent to parallelize our procedures, we noticed an increase in cost. When running a standard sequential stored procedure, BigQuery caches the base table for the first thread. However, splitting this logic into parallel streams can inadvertently negate those caching benefits, causing full table scans for each thread. To solve this, we asked the Data Engineering Agent to create materialized views for intermediate tables. These views effectively pre-cache the data, ensuring that your parallelized queries remain performant and cost-efficient. To make the agent parallelize the code more efficiently we gave it specific instructions on which areas (staging tables) we were interested in parallelizing. Results: Accelerated migration and performance Deploying Data Engineering Agent delivered immediate and measurable impact, specifically in addressing the toil associated with legacy migrations. The agent successfully achieved high-fidelity replication of all stored procedures, ensuring 1:1 logic parity with minimal human intervention. By automating the conversion of complex ETL pipelines, the agent achieved a 90% reduction in migration time compared with traditional manual approaches. What would have typically required weeks of engineering effort was completed in a fraction of the time, freeing engineers to focus on other key tasks. Furthermore, the modernization of the underlying infrastructure resulted in substantial performance gains. Post-migration benchmarks indicate that the new data pipelines run twice as fast , significantly reducing query latency and increasing overall data throughput. And as we previously discussed, instructing the agent to cache intermediate tables led to a 30% reduction in costs . Beyond accelerating development and reducing costs, these agentic tools are also changing the way data engineers approach their work. Rather than spending significant time on repetitive migration and optimization tasks, engineers can collaborate with agents to explore different implementation options, validate design decisions, and accelerate delivery. This shift is encouraging teams to adopt new ways of working, where agentic capabilities become an integral part of the development process and help shape how data solutions are designed, delivered, and maintained. Industrializing the Data Engineering Agent at Vodafone At Vodafone, we’re planning to scale the use of the Data Engineering Agent across the company in the following key areas: Standardized Dataform template repository: Establishing a central repository for Dataform templates allows for consistent architecture and design patterns across different projects and teams, helping ensure quality and alignment with global standards. Global market onboarding: We will expand the Data Engineering Agent deployment across key Vodafone markets including the Czech Republic (CZ), Romania (RO), Ireland (IE), Germany (DE), and the United Kingdom (UK), to drive widespread adoption and modernization. Integration with developer environments (IDEs): Deepening the integration of agentic capabilities directly into developer workflows (such as VS Code, and and Antigravity) will enable engineers to leverage Data Engineering Agent features within their existing tools and IDEs. Federated CI/CD governance: Implementing a centralized yet flexible governance framework for Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) will allow individual markets to maintain autonomy while adhering to corporate quality and security policies. Modernization of legacy stored procedures at scale: By systematically migrating complex, legacy workloads — specifically SAS code, BTEQ scripts, and MicroStrategy — into modern Dataform pipelines will allow us to reduce technical debt and accelerate transformation across the enterprise. To learn more about transforming your enterprise data architecture for the agentic era, download our complete Data Agents Guidebook or explore Google Cloud’s Rapid Migration and Modernization Program (RaMP) . To get started building and optimizing your own data pipelines with the agent today, visit the Data Engineering Agent pipelines documentation .

title: Introducing ambient networking for GKE
raw_text: Network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment. Today, we are announcing the general availability of ambient networking for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). This milestone marks an important evolution in how your run service mesh on GKE, bringing a sidecar-less architecture into production. Introduced earlier this year, ambient networking decouples functionality traditionally provided as a service mesh from application workloads, allowing platform operators and developers to help secure, observe, and route traffic without the resource overhead and operational complexity of managing sidecar proxies. Ambient networking architecture The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services. Control plane The ambient networking control plane orchestrates operations across the cluster. Traffic Director: Serves as the centralized xDS control plane, continuously delivering routing rules, access control policies, and cluster state updates to node-level proxies. Certificate Authority Service: Authenticate workloads and dynamically issues managed workload identity certificates, on-demand to enable seamless mTLS encryption across service-to-service communication. GKE control plane: Manages the cluster Gateway controller: Reads the Gateway CRDs and passes configuration information to Traffic Director GKE node components At the same time, several Node-level management components operate securely within the gke-managed-ambient namespace: Ambient networking runtime interface (NRI) plugin: Integrates with the NRI to perform low-level network redirection, intercepting traffic to and from ambient-enabled application pods. xDS agent (ambient agent): Runs inside the node proxy pod to receive xDS configuration updates from Traffic Director and request certificates from the GKE control plane on-demand. Node proxy (L4 Envoy proxy): A high-performance, shared per-node Envoy instance that processes intercepted L4 traffic, enforces mutual TLS (mTLS), evaluates authorization policies, performs load balancing, and emits rich telemetry metrics. Service pods: The user’s application/service pods communicate through the GKE node proxy to perform service to service mTLS across the cluster. Core functionality Together, these features combine to deliver a number of advanced capabilities for GKE environments: Zero Trust architecture: Ambient networking allows customers to establish a Zero Trust security posture. Traffic between workloads can be automatically encrypted using mutual TLS (mTLS) with managed workload identities, helping protect and secure service-to-service communication across the cluster. Simplified access policy: Granular control over service communication is simplified through authorization policies. Operators can define precise access rules to enforce least-privilege security boundaries between microservices. Rich telemetry: Gain operational insights with out-of-the-box L4 metrics and L7 metrics. Observability data can be collected automatically, giving teams visibility into traffic patterns, latency, and connection health for efficient monitoring and troubleshooting. To see these metrics, use Network Services Monitoring, a new Google Cloud capability that is also available today. Network Services Monitoring shows the traffic that ambient networking handles, for example, service-to-service connections, latency, and error rates, across your GKE clusters, so you can understand service dependencies without building your own dashboards. To learn more, read the documentation . Ambient networking benefits Ambient networking delivers tangible value for GKE operators: Simpler operations : Traditionally, service mesh products rely on injecting sidecar containers directly into every workload pod. Ambient networking removes this sidecar dependency by shifting networking features to shared node components. This fully managed solution simplifies deployment and streamlines day-to-day cluster operations. Simplified lifecycle management: When proxy logic is decoupled from application containers, lifecycle management is simplified. Upgrading proxy versions or applying configuration updates helps avoid restarting application workloads or scheduling downtime windows, enabling continuous availability for your services. Ambient networking can reduce administrative overhead and application disruption an average of four times annually by eliminating pod restarts required by CVE patches for L4 mesh usage. This fully managed solution can be installed either at cluster creation time or added to an existing cluster. Ongoing maintenance to the cluster components is handled by automated systems and is performed along with normal GKE cluster maintenance. Reduced resource consumption: By moving away from sidecar proxies for each pod, ambient networking reduces compute and memory overhead. Ambient networking enables up to a 10x reduction in GKE resource usage for layer 4 (L4) mesh features, including mTLS, load balancing, telemetry, and more. Try ambient networking in your GKE clusters today Simplifying adoption by removing the cost and complexity barriers of sidecars. Try it out in your GKE environment and experience the benefits of ambient networking: fully managed installation and upgrades service-to-service mTLS and authorization policies lower resource usage than sidecars L4 & L7 metrics See our documentation for more information: https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ambient-overview Pricing: https://cloud.google.com/products/gke-service-networking/pricing

title: How to simplify cloud access with Unified Access Policies, now in preview
raw_text: As organizations scale their cloud footprint to thousands of autonomous agents and microservices, you can accidentally create an operational bottleneck with strict Identity and Access Management (IAM). Meanwhile, administrators still need to enforce least privilege across thousands of resources without slowing down engineering velocity. Enter Unified Access Policies (UAPs), Google Cloud's next-generation access control engine in Cloud IAM , now in preview at no additional cost. UAP consolidates allow and deny rules into one unified schema, and decouples policy definition from resource enforcement. This approach allows you to author a policy once and bind it across your organization. UAP governs human, workload, and first-class agent identities with your existing IAM policies. With UAP, you can radically simplify your access policies and manage them more easily at scale. Scale limitations of legacy access models Traditional access policy models can push teams into a tough trade-off between Zero Trust access and pipeline speed due to three compounding forces: Fragmented schemas and permission sprawl : In granting thousands of granular permissions across cloud resources, administrators are forced to choose between either over-granting permissions from coarse roles with broad access, or wrangling two different syntaxes (APIs and mental models across allow and deny) just to define one workload's custom access posture. Policies treated as snowflakes : Because legacy policies attach directly to individual resources, applying a standard developer or security baseline across 25 projects means duplicating and maintaining 50 separate allow and deny policy configurations in Terraform. This approach can create severe configuration fatigue and operational burden, with greater risk of misconfiguration. Scale ceilings and explosion of agent identities : Modern cloud environments span human teams, federated workloads, service accounts, and autonomous agents that should never share generic service account credentials. As non-human and agent identities multiply, large enterprises routinely hit the hard 64 KB single-policy size limit on allow policies — requiring policy refactoring to onboard new teams or agents. Helping platform and security teams address these access limitations demands a new approach: an agent-ready engine on a unified control plane, designed to simplify, centralize, and scale access control. Key capabilities in UAP preview UAP removes cognitive burden for platform and IAM administrators, security architects, and agent administrators while shrinking your Infrastructure as Code footprint. UAP re-architects how policies are authored, bound, and enforced across your resource hierarchy because it’s built around a simpler authorization model. 1. Unified allow and deny syntax : Consolidate positive access grants and firm security guardrails into a single, auditable policy instead of reconciling separate allow and deny files. 2. Multi-binding support : A standalone policy binding acts as the connective tissue between your policy definition and target Cloud Resource Manager (CRM) nodes (organization, folder, and project). You can now bind a single UAP policy across up to 25 CRM targets in preview, eliminating duplicate Terraform blocks. 3. Expanded scale limits (5x effective policy size) : UAP breaks through the legacy single-policy size ceiling by letting you attach up to five UAP policies (64 KB and up to 100 rules each) to any single CRM resource — scaling to 2,500 unique principals and 500 groups per resource. 4. Clear separation of concerns : Central security architects can author vetted baseline and guardrail policies at the organization node and delegate self-service binding to folder and project administrators, without letting local teams alter central rule logic. 5. Expressive permission wildcards and immutable guardrails : Replace brittle permission lists with prefix, suffix, and substring wildcards alongside predefined roles and action exclusions (excluded permissions). 6. Built-in readiness for agents : UAP treats agents as first-class principals ( principal://agents.global... ) rather than generic service accounts. Agent administrators can scope least-privilege allow and deny rules directly to individual agents or entire agent pools, combine UAP with short-lived, downscoped tokens, and build on an extensible foundation for human-in-the-loop and delegated agent authorization. 7. Day 1 parity across all four surfaces : At runtime, Cloud IAM evaluates your existing allow policies, deny policies and UAP policies concurrently across your resource hierarchy. Whether your teams prefer interactive workflows or declarative automation, UAP launches with full create, read, update, and delete parity across the Google Cloud console, gCloud CLI, Terraform, and the Cloud IAM v3 REST API. You can deploy your first policy to bring these powerful capabilities into your environment in just a few minutes. Enforce UAP in 3 steps While you can automate UAP through Terraform, gCloud CLI or REST API, you can also author and bind policies interactively in the Google Cloud console. Step 1: Open the Unified Access Policies tab In the Google Cloud console, select your target organization, folder, or project in the resource picker and navigate to IAM & Admin > IAM . Alongside the existing Principals tab, select the new Unified Access Policies tab to view all policies in your scope — including their binding status, governed principals and rule types — and click + Create policy . Unified Access Policies page lists all the policies managed at/ enforced at the scope picked by the customer (Project, Folder or Org). Step 2: Define policy details and access rules In the Policy Details pane, enter a policy name and description, then build your access posture under Add rules : Select principals and exceptions : Choose a principal set or individual identity (such as dev group or agent identity) via + Add principal , and optionally exempt breakglass administrator groups via + Add exception principal. Choose the rule effect and permissions : Select Allow (using predefined roles, individual permissions or permission wildcards) or Deny (using explicit permissions or wildcards, such as compute.googleapis.com/firewalls.* ) Combine rules in one policy : Click Add another rule to pair positive grants and deny guardrails in the same policy, while inspecting the live JSON configuration preview on the right. Create Allow and/or Deny rules within a single UAP policy resource. Step 3: Bind the policy and manage lifecycle Proceed to the Enforcement step, select the target organization, folder, or project scopes where you want the policy to take effect, and click Bind policy . Once created, you can click any policy on the Unified Access Policies landing page to open its Policy details view — where you can audit active rules and resource bindings, click View JSON to export the policy for IaC pipelines, or edit bindings as your environment evolves. Every policy can be bound to a target resource through a binding. Leveraging separate bindings, a single policy can be enforced on multiple resources, unlocking simpler management at scale. With your first policy securely enforced and managed, your security and platform teams can spend less time wrangling permission sprawl and more time driving business velocity. Get started today With Unified Access Policies, we are excited to help you build a more secure, agile and future-ready cloud architecture that scales alongside your human and AI workloads. To streamline your organization’s access management, explore the Unified Access Policies documentation , and try it in a test project — create and bind your first reusable UAP policy using gcloud CLI, REST API, or Terraform.
summary: As organizations scale their cloud footprint to thousands of autonomous agents and microservices, you can accidentally create an operational bottleneck with strict Identity and Access Management (IAM). Meanwhile, administrators still need to enforce least privilege across thousands of resources without slowing down engineering velocity. Enter Unified Access Policies (UAPs), Google Cloud's next-generation access control engine in Cloud IAM , now in preview at no additional cost. UAP consolidates allow and deny rules into one unified schema, and decouples policy definition from resource enforcement.

title: The Blueprint: How Kult built a gaming companion that actually knows your game
raw_text: Welcome to The Blueprint , our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work. Kult is a London-based startup building a companion experience for games. It sits alongside your session, understands the game you are playing and where you are in it, and answers by voice and on a second screen. The more you play with it, the better it knows how you like to play. The challenge Traditionally, getting help in the middle of a game meant alt-tabbing, opening a video, scrolling a forum, and hoping you find the answer before you forget why you looked. Information should come to the player instead. As gamers ourselves, our team wanted a way for someone to be able to ask a question out loud, hands on the keyboard or controller, hear an answer, and consult a second screen if needed, without interrupting their immersion in the game. Three things decide whether that works: latency, accuracy and cost. Latency: Games are time-sensitive. The answer has to be fast, and the interaction should feel like asking a friend who’s an expert on the game, sitting on the couch next to you and watching you play. Accuracy: General-purpose models have training cutoffs. They can be months out of date and are often wrong about a specific game, patch, or build — and a wrong answer can be costly in the game and a waste of the player's time. Every game also has its own items, systems, and vocabulary, so accuracy has to hold across hundreds of games. The right answer also depends on the player: The same question deserves a different answer 10 minutes into a game than a 100 hours in. Cost: An always-on companion handles many turns per session, so every turn has to be inexpensive enough for a consumer product. Covering hundreds of games is only possible if adding one is cheap and takes no manual work. The solution Given these needs, we knew we would want a range of models to build Kult. Fortunately, Google’s Gemini models have some of the greatest variety in terms of balancing performance and especially cost, and with the Model Garden in Gemini platform, we have access to hundreds of models beyond Gemini. Gemini models have became the default family on both sides of the system: the live conversation, and the knowledge behind it, dynamically match the right model for every task. aside_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('title', 'In the Clouds with... Omid Ashtari'), ('body', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5582c76e50>), ('btn_text', 'Read it now.'), ('href', 'https://cloud.google.com/transform/in-the-clouds-omid-ashtari-kult-gg-interview-ai-companion-for-gamers'), ('image', <GAEImage: omid-ashtari-kult-gg-in-the-clouds-portrait>)])]> The lightest Gemini Flash tier handles high-volume, repetitive work, where we make thousands of small calls for every game we add. Gemini Flash runs every conversational turn. It works out what the player is asking and writes an answer grounded in our knowledge of that game, fast enough to keep up with play. The latest and most advanced Gemini models handle the rare, heavy reasoning we do once per game. Having that range on one API surface matters to a small team. The latest Gemini Flash models in particular sit at a point of price, speed, and quality that we have not found elsewhere, and they are the reason an always-on gaming companion works as a consumer product. We reach the models through both the Gemini platform and the Gemini Developer API , with a routing layer that picks the backend for each model. Our backend runs on Google Kubernetes Engine . Every answer comes in two parts. The voice gives the short version. At the same moment, a visual answer lands in a feed on the player's second screen: images, embedded video, maps, builds, interactive tools made for that game, and links to the guides and creators behind the answer. We build that feed with Google's open standard for agent-generated interfaces. The model does not write code. It describes the interface it wants using a catalog of components we designed, and the app renders it natively in Kult's own style. That keeps the feed safe and consistent, and lets us add new kinds of visual answers, and new devices, without rebuilding the front end. The architecture The outcome Kult now covers more than 100 games, and adding a game is an automated process, not a manual project. That’s a key part of what lets a small team aim at any game a player picks up, including new releases, where most of the playing happens in the first weeks. We are in alpha with our first players and opening up to more over the coming months. As we have grown, we have built a close working relationship with the Google Cloud team, with direct access to their engineers when we need it. That matters when every model generation raises the ceiling of what a gaming companion product can do. This expertise, both within the models and our supportive partners, allows us to focus on our passion: building the features gamers want, faster and better than any possible competition. The details Five principles shape how Kult works. Answers come from knowledge we build, not from what a model happens to remember. A game can change with every patch. For each game we cover, Kult builds a structured knowledge base automatically and keeps it current, and the model's job is to reason over that knowledge. The answer depends on who is asking. Kult keeps track of your session: the game, what you have been doing, and what you asked a moment ago. "What is he weak to?" needs no further explanation, because Kult already knows which boss you’re facing. Over time it learns from how you play, what you ask about and what you ignore, and shapes its answers around you. A player who wants the fastest route and one who wants to find everything should not get the same replies. The player is never left in silence. Kult responds straight away and carries the conversation while the deeper reasoning runs behind it. The spoken answer is short, and the visual feed carries everything the voice cannot. The smallest model that can do the job does the job. Much of the work in a system like ours is a decision, not a piece of writing. It needs to understand which game the query is about, does the question need a lookup, did the answer cover the point. For decisions like these we use Jev , a decision-only model that returns a choice with a calibrated confidence score. Confident cases are settled in a fraction of a second at a fraction of the cost, and uncertain ones escalate to a larger Gemini model. Every model sits behind a registry, so when a new generation ships, we benchmark it against reference answers written by people who know the games, and swap it in if it wins. Every question makes Kult better. Taken together, the questions players ask about a game show us where its knowledge is thin and what to build next. We are designing Kult so that this loop tightens with every session. The more people play, the richer the knowledge becomes for everyone. Every session teaches a player something, as well as the entire Kult system, and Kult helps them keep it. We think the companion that sits beside the game is only the start. Next is computer vision. In the coming months, Kult will start to see what is happening in your game, so the companion can be aware of the moment without being asked. We’re using Google's Live models as part of that work, for video understanding and more. If you are a gamer, try it for yourself www.joinkult.gg

In the latest AI Agent Clinic episode, Google Cloud engineer Laxmi Harikumar and developer Miles Libbey add long term memory to a voice agent built with Agent Development Kit (ADK). Cut background agent costs in half with the deferred tier on Gemini platform The deferred service tier is generally available (GA) on the Gemini platform for the Interactions API , Agent Development Kit (ADK) , and Deep Research . Running multi-hour background loops through synchronous real-time inference introduces unnecessary cost and triggers 429 resource exhaustion errors at peak. Static batch inference offers a 50% discount only when all prompts sit in a fixed input file upfront, which breaks dynamic tool loops. On the Gemini platform, the new deferred service tier brings batch economics to dynamic, stateful, multi-turn agents. Instead of competing with live chat traffic, the scheduler routes latency-tolerant agent turns to spare global capacity at half the cost. Set service_tier="deferred" in ADK RunConfig or client.interactions.create() across gemini-4-argon, gemini-4-carbon, gemini-3.x models, and gemini-deep-research-1.0. Read the guides for the Interactions API , ADK , and Deep Research . 50% discount and cache savings: Completed turns receive 50% off Standard PayGo rates and stack with prompt caching. title: Introducing object enrichments: Transform unstructured data into agent-ready context
raw_text: The vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files. This data holds the institutional knowledge AI agents need to do business-critical work. But to an agent, a raw object is just bytes it can't reason over. As enterprises start to deploy agents in production, the focus has shifted toward transforming these raw objects into rich, agent-ready context. Today, we are introducing object enrichments , a new Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context , enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions. Object enrichments gives customers access to the AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling at 75% cost savings when compared to similar services from other cloud providers . Available in preview, this fully managed service also includes high-quality PDF classification model, enabling customers to seamlessly turn their object store into an intelligent, AI-ready foundation. “L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex. Cloud Storage object enrichments’s high quality and cost-effective annotations enable us to discover, understand, and govern our content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. Object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes. ” – Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect, L’Oreal Agents need context, not raw bytes To operate efficiently, agents need grounded knowledge; however, reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive. For example, if an operations agent needs to pinpoint a specific event—such as a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard—streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames into the AI model on every user prompt would burn through expensive tokens and add minutes of delay. To bridge this gap, teams must pre-process raw data and extract rich, contextual metadata, which agents can then leverage at runtime. Historically, achieving this meant dealing with three challenges: Cost: Running models over millions to billions of objects is expensive, pushing organizations to compromise and process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots that lessen agents’ accuracy. Operational toil: A self-managed pipeline means stitching together multiple services — from event triggers and queues to custom infrastructure built on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — along with scalable retry/error logic and job scheduling. Once deployed, that infrastructure still requires continuous upgrades and capacity management. Teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing rather than focusing on building agents that solve actual business problems. Fragmented metadata: Extracted metadata often lands in a separate data store, decoupling context from the bytes it describes. Teams must pay for and maintain a second storage system, govern access policies across disconnected permission models, and run custom cleanup jobs to keep metadata in sync when source objects are copied, moved, or deleted. This is why we built object enrichments: to natively provide agent-ready context for your unstructured data, equipping your agents with complete, grounded knowledge without prohibitive costs, custom pipeline plumbing, or fragmented metadata. Key benefits of object enrichments 1. Reduce costs with Google models Object enrichments offers dramatic savings at scale: enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 (according to published pricing). You can use Google’s high-quality AI models for image annotations—including object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection—at one of the industry’s best price points. In addition, the PDF classification model lets you categorize documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health. "Even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy, while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x. ” – Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships, Hyperscience 2. Generate richer context with Gemini For complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, you can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments, unlocking advanced use cases such as summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Please reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality. 3. No pipeline, low toil setup Skip the brittle, multi-component DIY pipelines. Setting up an enrichment job just takes three simple steps, with no code required in the Google Cloud console, or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API, following these steps: Define your scope: Provide a set of buckets containing the objects to process and specify the processing location. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects. Choose your models: Pick one or more of the five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs. Grant permissions: Grant the necessary IAM permissions to the object enrichments service to access your Cloud Storage buckets. Object enrichments handles the rest: It orchestrates model inference, parses the responses, and writes the results to each object's object context, with built-in retries and throttling. There are no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain. "Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery, slashes AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving our models." - Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI, Vivint 4. Context lives where the bytes live Instead of parking metadata in a separate data store, object enrichments writes model outputs directly to object context , a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct that’s purpose-built for storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object itself. Because context is stored alongside object’s actual bytes, you get enterprise-grade data management out of the box, with: Cloud Storage durability and simplified lifecycle management: Object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object. It travels automatically with the object during copy, move, and replication operations and is automatically removed when the object is deleted — no more cleanup jobs! Fine-grained IAM governance: Using IAM, administrators can control who can read, add, update, or remove object context. Fast object filtering and serving: Applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects, in order to serve richer experiences. Turnkey multimodal analytics in BigQuery : You can easily configure your object context to natively flow into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets , allowing data teams to run SQL analytics, build dashboards, and join unstructured file insights with structured enterprise tables, without writing a single line of ETL code. What customers are building Early customers are already putting object enrichments to work across key business scenarios: Creative asset search and media archives: Marketing, retail, and media organizations manage petabytes of creative image assets, where finding a specific asset, e.g., "a red car driving at sunset" or "a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour", requires rich semantic metadata. Object enrichments automatically generates descriptive labels in object context, which can then be indexed into a vector database or BigQuery to power accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and asset-discovery agents. Automated trust, safety, and content moderation: Social platforms, marketplaces, and digital media pipelines scan millions of user uploads and supplier catalogs every day for explicit content. Historically, scaling this for every single upload has been cost-prohibitive, but not anymore. With object enrichments, you can process 10 million images for just $700. Training data curation for frontier AI: Autonomous driving, smart home, and robotics companies capture hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files. They often need targeted data samples for specific fine-tuning scenarios, which make up only a tiny fraction of their corpus. By enriching raw captures in place with object detection and image labeling models and then querying the resulting metadata in BigQuery, ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months. Multimodal analytics : Combine insights from images and documents with structured business data to drive personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery — for example, analyzing customer uploaded images of the product alongside their comments and recent sales data. Get started with object enrichments Object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. To get started, check out the following resources Read the documentation: Learn how to configure an enrichments job and use object contexts . Analyze in BigQuery: Set up Storage Insights datasets and query your enrichments alongside your BigQuery business data. Connect your agents: Pair object enrichments and object context with the Cloud Storage MCP server to give agents secure, IAM-scoped access to your data and its context. Review pricing: See Cloud Storage pricing for details. Gemini enrichments : Reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality. Start building: Head to the Cloud Storage console to enrich your first bucket in just three clicks.

title: Helping our partners market smarter, together, with Gemini
raw_text: At Google Cloud, our commitment to agentic transformation extends to everyone, including the partners who build and grow alongside us. Today, we are excited to introduce new Gemini-powered co-marketing capabilities directly within everyday go-to-market workflows for our partners. These new features enable partners to produce customized, brand-aligned joint assets in minutes, scaling campaign execution and driving pipeline more effectively. From marketing together to innovating together: Scaling impact with Gemini As technology evolves and customer expectations shift, marketers are no longer just producing campaigns. We’re building continuous, hyper-personalized, data-driven demand engines, and we’re doing it across an increasingly fragmented buyer journey. For our partner network, delivering on this expectation means solving a dual challenge: differentiating core offerings while articulating a unified vision with Google Cloud. Bridging that gap at enterprise scale requires more than incremental efficiency — it requires agentic agility to jointly create, adapt, and distribute stories together that resonate. Natural language analytics: Gain end-to-end visibility connecting marketing execution directly to tangible business outcomes. It allows us to do more with less while accelerating pipeline for our joint solutions" - Liana Shuma , Global Head of Technology Partnerships, Pigment Preserving the best of Partner Marketing Studio While the platform features powerful new tools, our core focus remains unchanged: helping you build your brand authority and generate pipeline demand. You will continue to find a curated content library structured specifically for you, highlighting top-performing campaigns aligned with Google Cloud strategic priority plays. Furthermore, high-value partner services remain readily accessible within the platform: Applying to host customer events directly inside a Google office. Requesting a Google Cloud speaker for your hosted events. Attending dedicated office-hours sessions with Google Cloud marketing experts. GTM Specialist, Tiger Analytics “We appreciate Google Cloud’s support with speakers for our events. Via direct browser link: Visit www.partnermarketingstudio.com directly. In addition to Partner Marketing Studio, we’re leveraging Gemini throughout the partner experience, including a revamped partner marketing funds experience to streamline activity planning, simplify pipeline reporting, and proactively validate required documentation before submission. We’ve seen Google Cloud experience tremendous growth in recent years, and a major part of that success has been the incredible work done by our partner ecosystem. Now, as we’re bringing the power of Gemini directly into your go-to-market workflows, we’re excited to take our work together to a whole new level. With AI at our side, and as one of our strongest offerings, it will be easier than ever to create, connect, and grow together.

title: Introducing in-place migration to GKE Dataplane V2
raw_text: GKE Dataplane V2 is Google Cloud’s next-generation networking dataplane for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter ( eBPF ) and open-source Cilium to replace traditional iptables routing and kube-proxy . We built GKE Dataplane V2 to meet the performance, scalability, and security demands of modern cloud-native workloads. GKE customers consistently tell us that while they want to adopt GKE Dataplane V2 for its performance and scale, migrating production clusters carrying stateful workloads and established IP allocations has been challenging, often requiring a disruptive parallel cluster setup. Today, we are pleased to introduce the preview of in-place migration , allowing you to transition eligible VPC-native clusters from GKE Dataplane V1 to GKE Dataplane V2 directly. Let’s take a look at what GKE Dataplane V2 brings to the table and how to start migrating your environment to it. Why GKE Dataplane V2? GKE Dataplane V2 is built on the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium, with features specifically tuned for performance, scalability, and deep integration with Google Cloud networking. Consider the following capabilities: Scale and performance: By handling packet processing with eBPF maps in the Linux kernel instead of linear iptables rules, GKE Dataplane V2 supports clusters of up to 15,000 nodes with network policy enforcement (and up to 65,000 nodes when network policy enforcement is disabled, which requires recreating clusters). This architecture also handles the high Pod churn, fast sandbox provisioning, and network identity scaling required by large agentic AI workloads . High-throughput accelerator networking: Serves as the foundational networking layer for GPU and Cloud TPU clusters on GKE, helping keep accelerators computing rather than waiting on network initialization. It also powers capabilities like GKE managed DRANET for Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) of network devices. Network security and observability: With GKE Dataplane V2, standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement and hierarchical ClusterNetworkPolicy work directly in the kernel with optimized performance. GKE Dataplane V2 also provides the underlying dataplane for sidecarless GKE ambient networking , while GKE Dataplane V2 observability delivers native network policy logging , live traffic topology, and Hubble flow metrics. The in-place migration workflow Instead of having to manually move workloads to a new cluster, GKE now automates the transition across three stages, as described in the GKE Dataplane V2 migration guide : 1. Eligibility and preflight checks: Before starting, verify that your Pod IP ranges have enough capacity to recreate the nodes by using GKE IP address utilization insights , and check Active Assist for incompatible configurations like custom eBPF programs on managed interfaces. 2. Initiate the migration: Once you’ve verified the preflight checks, start the migration with a single Google Cloud CLI update command. To initiate the migration on an eligible cluster, run: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER_NAME \\\r\n --location=LOCATION \\\r\n --enable-dataplane-v2'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5594542290>)])]> 3. Automated rollout and finalization: GKE updates your node pools to GKE Dataplane V2 while respecting your configured maintenance windows, exclusions, and upgrade strategies. To move faster, you can also patch specific node pools manually, or roll back to GKE Dataplane V1 at any time prior to finalization. In-place migration supports VPC-native clusters running GKE 1.35 or later (see the migration guide for exact version requirements). It does not support routes-based clusters or clusters running Calico. Get started In-place migration to GKE Dataplane V2 is available now in preview. During this time, we recommend testing migrations on non-production or test clusters first as you plan your broader transition. To learn more about GKE Dataplane V2 and to get started: Review cluster eligibility and migration phases in About migrating to GKE Dataplane V2 . Follow the instructions in Migrate VPC-native clusters to GKE Dataplane V2 . Read GKE Network Interface, from kubenet to eBPF/Cilium to DRANET for background on the evolution of GKE CNIs. Explore GKE networking dataplane for large agentic AI workloads to see how Dataplane V2 scales for large AI clusters.

title: Scaling workforce productivity and upskilling in the agentic era
raw_text: As state and local agencies modernize to meet evolving public needs, leaders have an unprecedented opportunity to empower and elevate their teams. Modernizing public sector operations starts with giving dedicated public servants the right tools to thrive. By replacing repetitive administrative routines with intuitive, intelligent workflows, agencies can free their staff to do what they do best: focus on high-impact problem-solving, build rewarding careers, and deliver responsive, compassionate services to the residents and communities they serve. Modernizing an agency workforce means transitioning employees from institutional systems to agentic platforms—redirecting their efforts away from manual administration and freeing up time for high-touch service delivery. By leveraging Google Cloud’s integrated stack to modernize daily operations, agency leaders can reliably meet regulatory requirements while creating the operational capacity to innovate, develop staff, and strengthen public trust. Empowering municipal teams: The City of Los Angeles Under the leadership of CIO Ted Ross, the City of Los Angeles addressed administrative constraints by deploying Google Workspace with Gemini across its entire 27,500-person municipal workforce. City employees now use agents to instantly synthesize large amounts of grant documents buried in silos and quickly rewrite public web copy for clearer readability. This digital companion allows city staff to step away from time-consuming administrative tasks and spend more time focusing on critical community service delivery, ensuring the city is operationally ready to host major global events like the 2028 Olympics and 2028 Paralympics. Retaining regional talent: The University of Hawaii The University of Hawaii needed a better way to keep local talent from leaving the islands. To build and retain regional talent, the university turned to BigQuery and Gemini —creating an automated, skills-first platform that helps match individuals with career opportunities. This solution maps student and faculty capabilities, matches individuals to academic roles and public research projects, and helps retain top talent. Overcoming timeline constraints: The Indiana Department of Transportation The Indiana Department of Transportation was issued an urgent executive mandate requiring a comprehensive review of complex legal contracts within a strict 30-day window. The agency deployed Gemini to securely ingest, parse, and analyze the state’s contract repositories. The automated system successfully isolated key legal parameters, saving 360 hours of highly skilled engineering labor and meeting the strict deadline. Scaling document ingestion: State of Maryland A similar transformation occurred within Maryland’s state agencies, where caseworkers navigating complex public benefits documentation spent hours indexing files and searching manual handbooks to find specific clause requirements. Maryland deployed Gemini and Gemini Notebook across its 40,000-person state workforce, establishing a secure framework to index and interact with state benefits compliance manuals. Caseworkers can now run plain-language queries to retrieve policy directives in seconds, drastically reducing the administrative processing times for residents. Celebrating the builders of the agentic enterprise Giving the public sector workforce a secure starting point for enterprise workflows streamlines routine processes, creating the space for employees to expand their skills and lead strategic mission priorities.
