title: States meet to discuss binding rules for autonomous weapons
raw_text:
Human rights campaigners are urging the international community to immediately begin negotiating legally binding rules for the use of autonomous weapons systems, as states assemble in Geneva for a global conference on the issue.

Between 17 and 20 November 2026, states will meet at the United Nations (UN)-convened Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) for its seventh conference, where they will discuss the potential regulation of Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) that can select and kill targets without human oversight or intervention.

Such systems are already being used on battlefields, particularly in the Russia-Ukraine conflict, where weapons powered by artificial intelligence (AI) have killed soldiers and civilians.

Speaking with New Scientist, CEO of Ukrainian drone manufacturer Aero Center Alexander Kokhanovskyy told the publication that a test of its fully autonomous drone capabilities in 2024 ended with the deaths of two Russian soldiers: “We just launch it and we know everything will be dead – everything that will be found there in this particular area will be dead.”

AI-powered targeting systems are also increasingly being used in other contexts, with devastating consequences.

It is now well-documented, for example, that the Israeli Defense Force (IDF) is using data analytics and AI-powered tools in Gaza to generate huge “kill lists” and make strike recommendations on an industrial scale.

One former Israeli intelligence officer told Israeli media outlet +972 that the IDF’s web of AI-powered targeting systems – including Lavender, Gospel and Where’s Daddy? – essentially work to facilitate a “mass assassination factory”.

In February 2026, the US military also relied on AI-powered targeting to strike 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours of its attacks on Iran. One of the targets hit was a school in Minab, which killed more than 120 children.

AI-enabled drone swarms have also been documented in Sudan, where they have been deployed as autonomous loitering munitions.

Potential negotiating positions

Ahead of the CCW conference, in September 2026, the 128 states parties to the CCW adopted by consensus the final report of the Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) on autonomous weapons, which sets out the “elements of a [legal] instrument, without prejudging its nature, and other possible measures to address LAWS”.

Some of the report’s proposed measures include full lifecycle testing of weapons systems, accountability arrangements that ensure human command and control, and placing operational guardrails on states deploying the technology.

The report also clarified that legal obligations apply to states and individuals, not machines, meaning legal liability for military actions cannot be transferred to autonomous systems.

It further noted that international humanitarian law (IHL) “governs the use of all weapons, means and methods of warfare, those of the past, those of the present, and those of the future, including those incorporating emerging technologies in the area of LAWS”.

However, while the vast majority of countries now support regulating autonomous weapons, a small number of countries – including the US, UK, Russia, India and Israel – remain steadfast in their opposition to new binding rules, arguing that existing ​humanitarian law is sufficient.

The US specifically favours voluntary guidelines, submitting a working paper to the CCW on 4 November 2026 that proposed five more years of consensus-based work towards a non-binding instrument. The paper further argued that the appropriate use of LAWS can “reduce the risks to civilians” compared with weapons that lack autonomous capabilities.

Given the overwhelming global consensus that autonomous weapons systems should be subject to new rules regulating their use, campaigners are urging states to “meet the moment” and agree to launch treaty negotiations immediately.

The outcome of the CCW conference will decide whether anyone who builds or fields AI-enabled targeting systems faces a legally binding international text, or only voluntary guidance. However, CCW decisions require consensus, giving any one government veto power over the discussions.

Inadequacy of IHL

According to León Castellanos-Jankiewicz, a senior researcher in International Law at the University of Amsterdam Faculty of Law and a non-resident fellow at the UN Institute for Disarmament Research, the increasing use of autonomous weapons presents difficulties for the application of international humanitarian law.

“Many AI-enabled weapons are black boxes. Given their ability to adapt in real time, machine learning systems are responsive to countless environmental stimuli. To achieve their goals, they can identify and exploit opportunities that their designers did not foresee, exhibiting what scientists describe as ‘emergent’ behavior. Put simply, their choices cannot be fully predicted or explained ahead of time as required by law,” he wrote in November 2026.

“Kill decisions are also deeply networked, arising from sensor and platform interaction rather than from a single, isolated judgment. In contrast, international humanitarian law assumes unity of purpose by treating each attack as flowing from a discrete decision; yet new technologies like drone swarms are decentralized by definition.”

Commenting on the latest CCW report drafted ahead of the conference in Geneva, Castellanos-Jankiewicz said although it is a good start, it fails to close the enforcement gap for weapons systems operating in unobserved environments.

“The report’s language covers human control before and during deployment. But once a drone is jammed, only inputs made prior to launch remain relevant for liability,” he wrote, adding that generally limited target verification and an inability to tie human intent to specific attacks makes it hard to apply accountability under international law as it is currently built.

“Worryingly, the text assigns no responsibility to the tech companies building these systems, who fiercely protect their commercial secrets from public scrutiny.

“This new algorithmic reality urgently needs new rules that reach beyond individual human intent: enforceable obligations for states that field unpredictable killing machines, and liability for the companies that build them.”

Calls for action

Campaign groups like the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Stop Killer Robots, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have all urged states party to the CCW to adopt a mandate for negotiations on a new legally binding protocol, which must be negotiated within one year – by the end of 2027.

“These new military tools pose potential threats to civilian protection and to long-standing, core principles of international humanitarian and human rights law. These weapons systems, or components, risk disproportionately harming populations that are already subject to greater violence and discrimination,” said Stop Killer Robots.  

“New international legal rules are the only logical and morally acceptable next step. Anything less would be unacceptably weak in the face of the clear and urgent dangers from autonomous weapons systems.”

It added that any legally binding instrument should contain both prohibitions and positive obligations. This should include prohibitions on weapons systems that target people, as well as those that do not allow for meaningful human control, and obligations to ensure all other systems are effectively controlled and understood.

“We are at a critical juncture. The vast majority of states worldwide are in favour of a new legally binding instrument on autonomous weapons systems,” said Nicole van Rooijen, executive director of Stop Killer Robots.

“This is urgently needed to ensure humans remain in control and accountable on the battlefield. Civilians must be better protected. States must adopt a negotiation mandate and a commitment to getting it done within one year.”

Verity Coyle, deputy director for arms in the crisis, conflict and arms division at Human Rights Watch, added that history will not judge states by how long they discussed LAWS, but by whether they acted before meaningful human control was lost.

“With reports of increasingly autonomous weapons already emerging from contemporary conflicts, governments face a clear choice: launch treaty negotiations now or allow the rules of war to be rewritten by technological developments and battlefield practice. Human lives are too important to leave to algorithms.”

The ICRC also said that a one-year negotiating mandate for a new protocol on autonomous weapons “would demonstrate that the Convention remains credible and capable of addressing contemporary challenges, while delivering on its fundamental promise: to alleviate human suffering in war”.

Read more about autonomous weapons

  • AI chooses nuclear escalation in 95% of simulated crises: With artificial intelligence increasingly deployed in analysis and decision-making in armed conflict, research shows AI systems will not naturally default to ‘safe’ outcomes in nuclear crises.
  • Lords split over UK government approach to autonomous weapons: During a debate on autonomous weapons systems, Lords expressed mixed opinions towards the UK government’s current position, including its reluctance to adopt a working definition and commit to international legal instruments controlling their use.

title: Beyond the skill library: Choosing expertise for agentic AI
raw_text:
It’s easy to create something that looks like an AI agent: give a model a prompt, connect it to a tool or a set of documents, and ask it to handle a task. The harder question is whether it knows what to do next, and if it’s using the right evidence.  When it doesn’t, failure is rarely obvious.  Instead, the agent gives a confident answer, and someone acts on it. 

Agentic skills are one way to close this gap between a plausible response and an answer grounded in the right evidence. A skill is more than a prompt, a document, or an application programming interface (API) call. At its best, it packages expertise into a reusable workflow: what information to gather, which tools to use, how to interpret the results, and what to do next.  

In practice, many skills describe the task but leave tool choice and result interpretation to the model, making outcomes less consistent. The agent coordinates the skills; the tools provide the capabilities, and the skills guide how they’re used. 

But simply giving an agent more skills won’t automatically make it more capable. What matters is whether it can compose the right skills around the intended outcome and use the skills selectively as the situation unfolds. 

From one broad skill to a coordinated investigation 

Consider a user who can connect to Wi-Fi but can’t start a video call. A skill built only to check wireless connectivity might confirm that the user is connected, but it won’t explain why the call isn’t working. The problem could involve wireless conditions, identity, DNS, routing, a service provider, or the application itself. 

A better approach starts with a broad troubleshooting skill that establishes what is happening: Is the issue real? Is it an outage or degraded performance? Who is affected? From there, the agent can call more focused skills to investigate the areas that fit the evidence. 

If one user is affected, for example, the agent might examine that user’s wireless connection and relevant access services, such as DHCP, DNS, or authentication. If those look healthy, it can follow the service path toward the application itself and examine relevant network and provider dependencies. If several users across a site are affected, the agent can skip the individual client checks and look at what those users share locally, such as the site’s DHCP, DNS, or authentication servers, or its security gateway. If users at several sites are affected, the common factor is more likely to sit centrally, in an identity provider, a load balancer, or the application itself. 

This is what nested, or composable skills make possible: a high-level skill coordinates more specialised capabilities, calling them when needed and carrying context from one step to the next. The agent doesn’t need to invoke every skill or run every test. It needs to connect relevant evidence across the service delivery chain, use normal results to rule out possible causes, and narrow down the likely fault domain. 

The value isn’t simply running more tests; it’s correlating the right evidence to understand the user’s experience. 

More skills can mean more failure modes 

 Adding a skill for every new gap can seem like the natural fix, but every skill an agent can access gives it another option to weigh. A large, flat library can slow the agent down and increase the chance it chooses the wrong skill. How each skill is scoped matters too. Skills that are too broad may not give the agent enough direction. Skills that are too narrow can proliferate into a collection of one-off workflows, while overlapping skills can direct an agent to the wrong tools or produce inconsistent results. 

Not every step in an investigation needs a skill or model reasoning, at all. Take a DHCP failure. An alert from the access point and a synthetic DHCP test from the same site provide independent signals. Simple rules can use those signals, along with how many clients are affected and whether the failure recurs, to determine whether the issue is isolated or site wide. For bounded, well-understood conditions like this, a deterministic check is often the better tool. It’s repeatable: the same evidence produces the same answer. It’s auditable: you can see which rule fired and why. And it’s grounded: actions can be tied to verified state rather than a model’s confidence. This isn’t the absence of expertise, but expertise hardened into rules once a problem is understood well enough.  

Skills earn their place when a problem is ambiguous and crosses domains, such as when dependencies span wireless, network, and application services. 

A single elaborate reasoning process for every task can add cost and delay without improving the answer. Skills should help define the appropriate path: what to check, when to expand the investigation, and when to ask a person to review the findings. 

DIY skills still need domain expertise 

Organisations will have good reasons to build some skills themselves. They understand their own applications, operating procedures, sites, and business constraints. That context can make an agent more useful. 

But generating a skill from documents, or asking a model to create one, is not the same as validating it. Does the skill call the appropriate tools? Are the results being interpreted correctly? Does it know what the evidence can and cannot establish? 

Those questions require domain expertise. In network operations, for example, a basic reachability check may show that a destination responds, but it may not establish whether users can actually join the call. Knowing which additional evidence to gather, and how to interpret it, takes expertise in the systems being investigated. 

A practical approach is to build around what is unique to the organization and use specialist capabilities where the work depends on trusted data and domain knowledge. An organisation might supply its own operational context while drawing on networking expertise and tools to investigate wireless, switching, identity, security, WAN, and application dependencies. 

Read more about AI amd agentic AI skills

  • Kaspersky to scan AI agents for backdoors as shadow AI spreads: The security supplier will release a tool this month that vets agent skills, models and artificial intelligence development components before they reach corporate networks to defend against threats from shadow AI.
  • Zoom debuts new agentic AI skills and agents for Zoom AI Companion: AI-first work platform provider expands agentic skills across the entire portfolio using reasoning and memory to take action and orchestrate task execution, conversational self-service and custom agent creation.

Make learning deliberate, too 

Past incidents can help an agent investigate future problems, but they shouldn’t automatically become new rules. Findings need to be checked and categorised before they are reused. Otherwise, an incorrect conclusion can be repeated until it appears authoritative. Even reviewed findings should point to where to look, not override what the live evidence shows.  

The same discipline applies to skills themselves. Organisations should evaluate them against realistic scenarios, confirm that they use the right tools and evidence, and test whether the right skill is selected for a given problem and whether it stays inactive when it isn’t needed. They should also verify that conclusions follow from the results, and that workflows are efficient, without unnecessary tool calls or model reasoning. Good output separates observations from inferences and states the likely fault domain, alternatives, confidence level, and recommended next checks to run. 

The future of agentic AI won’t belong to agents with the largest skill libraries. It will belong to agents that can assemble the right expertise, tools, and data for a specific outcome; carry context across the investigation; and know when they have enough evidence to act, and when to bring in a human.  

Mike Hicks is a principal solutions analyst at Cisco ThousandEyes

title: AI red team tool Artex likely behind cyber attack on EU body
raw_text:
Artex, an open source penetration testing framework powered by artificial intelligence (AI), may have been implicated in a cyber incident affecting the European Union’s (EU) executive body, the European Commission (EC) in Brussels.

The attack, which unfolded at the end of October, appears to have targeted the commission’s Sysper human resources (HR) platform, leaving staff unable to undertake some key tasks. The EC swiftly took down affected systems and Computer Weekly understands Sysper is back online at the time of writing, although, according to Euronews, other systems – including a health insurance program – are still offline.

Speaking on Thursday 19 November, the EC spokesperson for digital, Thomas Regnier, said: “The investigation is still ongoing. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings as they come…. We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole.”

The European Union’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said: “CERT-EU has observed similar instances of AI-driven activities against its constituency. These activities highly likely involved the use of Artex.”

ISACA chief global strategy officer Chris Dimitriadis said: “On the eve of the EU-UK summit, the news that the European Commission has suffered a significant cyber attack exposes Europe’s executive body. 

“While alarming, this attack is not surprising. Thanks to AI, attackers now hack at the speed of intent – a pace the public and private sector cannot outrun without serious investment in the cyber workforce. Until organisations deploy AI defensively as fast as criminals deploy it aggressively, we will continue on this trajectory. 

“In the short term, the commission will investigate whether staff data has been compromised and what weakness hackers were able to use Artex to exploit. They should be bolstering their cyber security and building long-term resilience by investing in recruiting, training and upskilling privacy professionals who can build defences that are stronger than the AI tools now freely available to attackers.” 

What is Artex?

At its core, the legitimate Artex framework consists of a large language model (LLM)-powered agentic platform, written in Go with a Next.js front end.

It can be used to automate offensive cyber tasks and was recently identified by threat intelligence teams and law enforcement agencies as increasingly finding favour among cyber criminals thanks to its ability to shrink the time needed to chain various offensive cyber tasks.

Indeed, some intrusions orchestrated using Artex are believed to have moved from initial targeting to full privileged access in less than three hours, moving up cyber attack timelines.

But its value to a threat actor lies not just in its speed, but in its scale and persistence as well. Artex is able to probe huge numbers of low-complexity issues, such as misconfigurations, that human eyes would miss, and of course it does not get tired or need tea breaks.

Microsoft said the tool was being heavily used by a Chinese state-aligned threat actor tracked as Storm-0940 to obtain access to its victims’ cloud infrastructure – including Microsoft 365 environments. Redmond’s findings have been corroborated by Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and its Mandiant stablemate.

Artex was first released on GitHub by a user known by the handle Autumn-27 in July of this year and reached between 1,500 and 2,000 users in the space of 10 weeks, according to the FBI in the US.

Autumn-27 had allegedly stated that Artex was supposed to be used for “authorised security testing” within defined scopes, and in fact pulled its repository on 8 October after reports that it was being abused.

Despite this, Artex persists and continues to proliferate through community forks, localised variants and a commercial version, Artex Pro.

CERT-EU said: “We assess that Artex’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors, resulting in more frequent, faster and more scalable automated attacks with a higher success rate.

“In April 2026, in our blog post AI is changing the economics of vulnerability discovery, we warned that autonomous offensive capabilities would progressively reach a wider range of actors. Artex is a concrete example of that shift materialising.”

Urgent steps for cyber teams

CERT-EU has made available a list of tasks for security teams to undertake to safeguard against Artex.

In the immediate future, priorities should be to audit publicly exposed IT assets and limit exposure; ensure management and control panels are isolated from the public internet or untrusted networks; prioritise emergency patching for all assets that must be exposed to the internet; and to monitor privileged and administrator account activity for evidence of suspicious behaviour or abuse.

In the short term, security teams should increase their use of multifactor authentication (MFA), and hunt for and alert on connections to known or suspected threat infrastructure to identify potential compromises, particularly artefacts and behaviours consistent with Artex. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools can also be pressed into service to block strange processes.

Security teams should continuously sanitise error responses from internet-exposed devices to minimise threat actor enumeration of their assets, protect said assets with web application firewalls (WAFs), adopt detection and logging best practices for incident response, ensure monitoring covers AI tools and assets using them, conduct regular vulnerability scans and penetration tests, and retain all findings – even those that don’t seem very severe – in the remediation cycle, which can help stop tools like Artex from chaining a series of minor problems into a great big one.

What next for Artex?

Looking ahead, Snehal Antani, CEO of Horizon3, said the clear jump in attack volume and velocity seen in recent weeks was likely attributable to frameworks like Artex and similar tools that enable bad actors to harness fleets of agents, essentially industrialising cyber attacks using proven, basic techniques.

“Artex and the forks that followed it are the multiplier. One operator can now run many targets in parallel, and the agents keep iterating even when the human walks away,” said Antani.

In emailed comments, Antani told Computer Weekly that Artex and similar frameworks will drive a type of attack standardisation that makes attribution much harder.

“When different groups – state-aligned or purely criminal – are all running near-identical agent harnesses, models and playbooks, their operational fingerprints start to look the same. You lose a lot of the traditional signals that used to separate actors.

“Going forward, expect this to become normal rather than exceptional. The skill barrier keeps dropping, the tooling keeps forking, and the economics favour volume. Organisations have significant cyber debt that is easily exploitable by frameworks like Artex, so we should expect persistent disruption of digital services – travel, banking, commerce, etc – in the coming months as these organisations scramble to quickly improve their cyber resilience.”

Antani warned that any defenders still inclined to treat exposure management as a quarterly scanning or annual penetration testing exercise will find themselves swiftly overwhelmed.

“Machine-speed offence is already here; machine-speed defence has to match it,” he said.

title: Over 250,000 Londoners affected by latest TfL breach
raw_text:
The personal information of approximately 265,000 bus, rail and tube passengers in London has been exposed in a new data breach at service operator Transport for London (TfL).

The data leak affected users of TfL’s Oyster photocards – which are provided to children and students, the over-60s, military veterans and people participating in apprenticeship schemes, among other things.

It is understood to include names, email and home addresses, phone numbers, birthdates and security questions, but not photos, passwords, financial details, or data relating to journeys made on London’s transport network.

TfL technology strategy and revenue director Shashi Verma said: “The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologise to our customers affected by this incident.”

TfL has taken the photocard system offline to prevent any malicious access and reported the incident to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). Affected users have also been contacted. It hopes to restore the service as soon as possible.

Speaking to the BBC, Verma revealed the breach came to light on Monday 16 November when photocard users received unexpected emails asking them to validate their TfL accounts, prompting an internal investigation.

In a statement, Verma said that the speed with which TfL had identified and closed down the attack meant its impact was more limited than it might otherwise have been.

He added that the compromised system had been subject to cyber security testing within the past 12 months, and pointed to the extensive work done in this regard following the 2024 Scattered Spider attack on its systems – for which two men were jailed earlier this year.

At the same time, he acknowledged that new hacking tools and techniques keep bubbling up, more so now than ever. “This is a very difficult game to keep up with,” he said.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, virtual chief information security officer (vCISO) and cyber security advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said: “265,000 people woke up to find their personal details in someone else’s hands through no fault of their own. Names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and security question answers.

“That last one matters more than most people realise. Security questions are reused across multiple accounts. Someone who knows your mother’s maiden name or your first pet now potentially has a key that works on more than just your Oyster account.”

Patel praised TfL for taking the system offline quickly, and said the fact that financial data or journey histories had not been compromised was good news.

Vulnerable targets

Although TfL has stated no data on any children was compromised in the latest incident, Comparitech security specialist Brian Higgins said the breach was significant because it included the data of more potentially vulnerable people, such as young adults who recently left foster care, and elderly people.

“It’s vital they understand how to protect themselves after a breach like this and TfL has a duty of care to ensure that they receive the best advice as swiftly as possible, especially since this has happened before,” said Higgins.

“Some well-publicised, customer-facing aftercare would help in this case, regardless of culpability. The US started enforcing financial sanctions paid to victims in data breaches many years ago. Perhaps the ICO should consider such measures in the UK, especially where incidents involving a finite and manageable victim pool like this present themselves. A little more data protection stick than carrot might shrink our digital attack surface,” said Higgins.

Patel added: “Public services hold significant volumes of personal data on millions of people, and the security investment protecting that data needs to match the trust citizens place in those services. TfL has been a cyber attack target before. The question the ICO will be asking is whether the lessons from previous incidents translated into the controls that should have made this one harder to execute.” 

Next steps

Oyster photocard users are being advised to change their login details and security questions immediately, and if those details have been used on any other online services, to rotate those credentials as well.

Users should also be on the lookout for suspicious contacts by email, phone or SMS in the coming days and weeks.

“If you hold an Oyster photocard, treat any unexpected contact referencing your account, your address, or your personal details with immediate suspicion regardless of how official it looks,” said Patel.

While the photocard system remains offline for the time being, users who need to renew their photocards imminently can reach out to TfL by telephone on 0343 222 1234.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) also produces guidance for individuals and families caught up in an incident, available here.

Read more about recent UK data breaches

  • Following a data breach earlier in October, cyber criminals appear to have a much more complete picture of Asos’ user base than first thought, it has emerged.
  • The UK’s Department for Education has disclosed a serious data breach orchestrated via a social engineering attack on its external-facing helpdesk.
  • A data breach affecting 138 members of the Civil Service Pension Scheme piles pressure on the service’s administrator, Capita, amid ongoing issues.

title: Ukrainian police arrest former members of Conti ransomware group
raw_text:
Ukrainian police have arrested four cyber criminals as part of an investigation conducted in cooperation with the FBI, claiming they are part of a much wider ransomware gang responsible for $40m of extorted funds from victims.

“The organisation comprises at least 27 people from different countries, including Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Russia. The associated broader criminal structure has more than 60 participants in eight jurisdictions. Among them are former members of the famous group of Conti hackers,” said a statement from the Ukrainian national police.

“At least 28 companies have transferred more than $40.5m in ransom to hackers,” they added. “The attackers stole 1.4 terabytes of data from a US company and extended the attack to other companies in the same group. Initially, they demanded $10m. Following the negotiations, they received $5m.”

The police said that, before being launched, “each attack [had] been carefully prepared. The attackers studied the company’s financial situation, assets, employees, and information system vulnerabilities. The targets were companies in the oil and gas, pharmaceutical, industrial and logistics industries, financial institutions and critical infrastructure facilities.”

This methodology is consistent with what has been known about the practices of the Conti gang since its disappearance in early 2022, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

“To access corporate networks, the authors posed as members of the IT support service, obtained login credentials and convinced employees to install remote access software,” the Ukrainian police said.

This practice refers to the BazarCall subgroup that specialised in establishing initial access to targeted systems for the benefit of two teams in particular within Conti - one that will have led to the Quantum ransomware, then Royal and BlackSuit, and the other leading to Black Basta, of which traces of former members have been found in other ransomware groups such as ThreeAM or Cactus.

According to Ukrainian police, cyber criminals have even “created their own platform with voice messages generated by artificial intelligence.” This suggests a BazarCall affiliation to Silent Ransom Group (SRG), whose internal leaks have recently been analysed by the Ransom-ISAC.

The infrastructure of the cyber criminal group BlackSuit was seized by law enforcement in July 2025, as part of an international operation called “Checkmate” - a valuable source of information that has potentially allowed authorities to identify other actors related to this group.

The operation was coordinated by Europol. The Ukrainian police helped confirm Quantum's affiliation to the Chaos group, passing through Royal and BlackSuit. Documents from Ukrainian court decisions provide elements confirming this assertion, openly mentioning Chaos.

Some US victims are explicitly named, starting with the Warren Oil Company, which is believed to have paid $5m in ransom in August 2024, but also Newpark Resources and Maxxis International, as well Quantum Health, which was attacked earlier this year. The Maxxis attack was claimed by the BlackSuit group in November 2024.

title: UK court confirms existence of government surveillance order against Apple
raw_text:
A British court has confirmed that the Home Office has issued a secret order to provide police and intelligence services with the capability to access encrypted data stored by users of Apple devices.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal found that government claims that confirming the existence of the order, known as a Technical Capability Notice (TCN), would damage national security were unfounded.

The tribunal rejected arguments from the Home Office that revealing the existence of the secret order, which has been widely reported in the press, and publicly referred to by senior members of the Trump administration, would damage national security. It found that the Home Office had failed to consistently follow its policy of neither confirming nor denying (NCND) the existence of the order, undermining government arguments that it should remain secret.

The case represents the second time this year that the government has been forced to back down on assertions of NCND to protect claimed government secrets. It follows the Agent X case, in which MI5 was found to have lied to two courts and misled an oversight body to protect a neo-Nazi informant who had abused his partner.

Existence of TCN already confirmed

Three judges found today (19 November) that despite the UK government’s claimed secrecy over the order issued to Apple, government officials had confirmed the existence of the TCN to newspaper journalists and to US government officials.

A leak to the Washington Post first revealed that the Home Office issued a technical capability notice to Apple in January 2025 requiring it to provide access to end-to-end encrypted messages and data stored by Apple’s customers worldwide in iCloud.

The existence of the order was confirmed by the former US director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, in a post on X in August 2025, which exceeded three million views, after the US administration raised concerns that the order would allow the UK to access data on American citizens.

The court also found that UK government officials gave briefings to the Times and the Financial Times confirming the existence of the secret order.

Apple, Privacy International and Liberty are challenging the home secretary’s legal powers to issue technical capability notices to technology companies in the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.

Apple’s legal arguments against the Home Office

Apple is bringing five core legal arguments challenging the home secretary’s powers to issue technical capability notices (TCNS) against tech companies:

  • Does the home secretary have powers to issue warrants for targeted interception of communications outside the United Kingdom?
  • Can the home secretary’s statutory powers be used to regulate security or privacy services offered by a technology company to its customers?
  • Was the consultation process which the Home Office is required to conduct before issuing a technical capability notice lawful?
  • Does the technical capability notice amount to disproportionate interference with people’s rights under the European Convention on Human Rights?
  • Has Apple been treated differently from other technology companies (for example, similar companies have not been issued with a TCN) by having a TCN issued against it?

The government can use TCNs to require tech companies to modify their services to provide police and intelligence services access to their users’ data. Rather than comply, Apple withdrew its Advanced Data Protection (ADP) service from UK users, stating: “We have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products and services and never will.”

The tribunal found that the government had not consistently applied its policy of neither confirming nor denying the existence of the order. Two different reputable newspapers had reported that government officials departed from NCND and positively confirmed the existence of the technical capability notice, it said.

Claims by the Home Office that internal leak investigations failed to find a government source that passed the information on to the press had “little or no evidential value”.

The home secretary had the opportunity to file detailed evidence about internal investigations to a closed hearing of the tribunal but had chosen not to do so, and ministers and government officials chose not to provide statements to the court.

Briefings to media and US officials

The judges inferred that the briefings to newspapers did take place and were authorised by government ministers, senior officials or special advisers.

“It is extremely unlikely that multiple government sources would have briefed the media in the absence of authorisation for such a briefing,” the court found.

The court also found that the UK government had given Apple permission to brief US government officials about the order, without any apparent assurance of confidentiality in what “amounted to a further clear departure from NCND”.

The court noted that it was “abundantly clear” by April 2025 that most senior US officials and politicians were not prepared to keep the order secret, as they regarded it as an “egregious breach” of US citizen’s First Amendment rights.

The cumulative effect was that anyone with even a passing interest in the topic would already know that the Home Office had served a technical capability notice on Apple, the judges found. Anyone could find out the answer to whether a TCN had been issued against Apple by simply typing the question into Google’s chatbot.

The judges agreed with Apple and the NGOs that the home secretary had not established that it would be damaging to national security to confirm the existence of the technical capability notice. The decision will mean that the court will be able to hear arguments over the lawfulness of the home secretary’s powers to issue TCN’s in public hearings.

Judges will decide whether details about the technical capability notice can be disclosed without damaging national security or the public interest in future hearings.

Apple is challenging the lawfulness of the home secretary’s powers to issue TCNs under five grounds (see box). Most of the arguments can be heard in open court without damaging national security, the IPT found today.

Caroline Wilson Palow, legal director at Privacy International, said that the decision was a major victory for transparency and effective oversight, adding: “The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rightly rejected the UK government’s attempts to shield from scrutiny an issue of immense public interest – whether Apple has been ordered to undermine the security of our devices – based on an unsupported claim of a risk to national security. The government should not be allowed to use its policy of ‘neither confirm nor deny’ as an impenetrable shield.”

Akiko Hart, director of Liberty, said that end-to-end encryption was vital to protect personal information and to securely communicate.

“Encryption protects the things that matter most to us – including our family photos, personal messages, bank details and health records. At a time of growing cyber threats, governments should be rising to the challenge to strengthen digital security protections rather than opening the door to hackers and hostile actors,” she added.  

A Home Office spokesperson confirmed the existence of the TCN, saying that the right to privacy should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public: “Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

“Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies,” the spokesperson added.

Timeline of UK government’s order for backdoor access into Apple’s encrypted iCloud service

  • 7 February 2025: Tech companies brace after UK demands backdoor access to Apple cloud – The UK has served a notice on Apple demanding backdoor access to encrypted data stored by users anywhere in the world on Apple’s cloud service.
  • 10 February 2025: Apple: British techies to advise on ‘devastating’ UK global crypto power grab – A hitherto unknown British organisation, which even the government may have forgotten about, is about to be drawn into a global technical and financial battle, facing threats from Apple to pull out of the UK.
  • 13 February 2025: UK accused of political ‘foreign cyber attack’ on US after serving secret snooping order on Apple – US administration asked to kick UK out of 65-year-old UK-US Five Eyes intelligence sharing agreement after secret order to access encrypted data of Apple users.
  • 14 February 2025: Top cryptography experts join calls for UK to drop plans to snoop on Apple’s encrypted data – Some of the world’s leading computer science experts have signed an open letter calling for the home secretary to drop a controversial secret order to require Apple to provide access to users’ encrypted data.
  • 21 February 2025: Apple withdraws encrypted iCloud storage from UK after government demands ‘backdoor’ access – After the Home Office issued a secret order for Apple to open up a backdoor in its encrypted storage, the tech company has instead chosen to withdraw the service from the UK.
  • 26 February 2025: US intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard probes UK demand for Apple’s encrypted data – A secret order issued by the UK against Apple would be a ‘clear and egregious violation’ if it provides backdoor access to Americans’ encrypted data, says US director of national intelligence.
  • 5 March 2025: Apple IPT appeal against backdoor encryption order is test case for bigger targets – The Home Office decision to target Apple with an order requiring access to users’ encrypted data is widely seen as a ‘stalking horse’ for attacks against encrypted messaging services WhatsApp, Telegram and Signal.
  • 11 March 2025: Secret London tribunal to hear appeal in Apple vs government battle over encryption – A secret tribunal is due to meet at the High Court in London to hear tech giant Apple appeal against a Home Office order to compromise the encryption of data stored by its customers on the iCloud service worldwide.
  • 13 March 2025: US Congress demands UK lifts gag on Apple encryption order – Apple and Google have told US lawmakers that they cannot tell Congress whether they have received technical capability notices from the UK.
  • 14 March 2025: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal holds a day-long secret hearing into an appeal brought by Apple against a government notice requiring it to provide law enforcement access to data encrypted by its Advanced Data Protection service on the iCloud, despite calls for the hearing to be open to the public.
  • 24 March 2025: Gus Hosein, executive director of Privacy International – Why I am challenging Yvette Cooper’s ‘secret backdoor’ order against Apple’s encryption.
  • 31 March 2025: Apple devices are at ‘most risk’ in UK following government ‘backdoor’ order, Lord Strasburger tells the House of Lords as a Home Office minister declines to give answers.
  • 2 April 2025: Apple has appealed to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal over an order by home secretary Yvette Cooper to give the UK access to customers’ data protected by Advanced Data Protection encryption. What happens next?
  • 7 April 2025: Investigatory Powers Tribunal rejects Home Office arguments that identifying the ‘bare details’ of legal action by Apple would damage national security, leaving open the possibility of future open court hearings.
  • 15 April 2025: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal is a semi-secret judicial body that has made significant legal rulings on privacy, surveillance and the use of investigatory powers. What does it do and why is it important?
  • 5 June 2025: US politicians are calling for Congress to rewrite the US Cloud Act to prevent the UK issuing orders to require US tech companies to introduce ‘backdoors’ in end-to-end encrypted messaging and storage.
  • 11 June 2025: Government using national security as ‘smokescreen’ in Apple encryption row – Senior conservative MP David Davis says the Home Office should disclose how many secret orders it has issued against telecoms and internet companies to Parliament.
  • 11 June 2025: WhatsApp seeks to join Apple in legal challenge against Home Office encryption orders – WhatsApp today applied to intervene in an Investigatory Powers Tribunal case that is considering the UK’s ability to issue a technical capability notice on Apple to ‘weaken encryption’.
  • 12 June 2025: Apple encryption row: Does law enforcement need to use technical capability notices? History shows that law enforcement can bring successful prosecutions without the need for the Home Office to introduce ‘backdoors’ into end-to-end encryption.
  • 21 July 2025: UK may be seeking to pull back from Apple encryption row with US – UK government officials say that attempts by the Home Office to require Apple to introduce ‘backdoors’ to its secure encrypted storage service will cross US red lines.
  • 23 July 2025: WhatsApp is refused right to intervene in Apple legal action on encryption ‘backdoors’ – Investigatory Powers Tribunal to hear arguments in public over lawfulness of secret UK order requiring Apple to give UK law enforcement access to users’ encrypted data stored on the Apple iCloud.
  • 19 August 2025: US says UK has agreed to drop encryption ‘backdoor’ demands against Apple – US and UK end diplomatic row over UK encryption ‘backdoor’ order against Apple, but it remains unclear whether Apple will restore advanced encryption services to UK users.
  • 29 August 2025: Home Office ‘backdoor’ seeks worldwide access to Apple iCloud users’ data, court documents confirm – A court filing states that a government order against Apple would give it the capability to access communications and metadata of customers using the iCloud service anywhere in the world.
  • 1 October 2025: Home Office issues new ‘backdoor’ order over Apple encryption – A second Home Office technical capability notice requires Apple to provide access to encrypted data and messages of British users stored on its iCloud service
  • 7 October 2025: Our phones as our castles: can His Majesty’s Government enter? – Ancient laws secure the sanctity of even the most humble of homes from government intrusion. How do they fare in an age of digital technology?
  • 13 October 2025: Court dismisses Apple’s appeal against Home Office backdoor – Court dismisses Apple’s appeal against Home Office backdoor
